utterances.text: One other matter before I invite Mr. Zecevic to begin. I would just remind to counsel as to today's sitting times. We would take the first break at 11.30 and the second session will run from 11.50 to 1.20, and the lunch break would be for an hour, and then we sit from 2.20 to 3.50 and the -- extended sessions takes us from 4.10 to 5.40. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday at the very end of the sitting, I said what our closing arguments are going to address. Before I go into detail, let me make a few preliminary remarks. Everything that the Defence announced in the opening statement was presented to the Trial Chamber and proven beyond doubt. A detailed analysis of all the evidence and laws adduced was presented in our final brief. Crucially, to this day, ever since Mico Stanisic was interviewed in 2007, his Defence has not departed from its initial position by a single centimetre. The statement made by Stanisic in the course of the five days of the interview with the Prosecution, what the Defence announced they would present in their opening statement, as well as the positions advanced at trial, they were all proven beyond doubt without any vacillation or variation, alternative explanations, or similar. We were full consistent in our position. I underscore this because the OTP position was quite the opposite. They advanced different positions at trial. They presented alternations of different positions, alternations of explanations, and alternations of their entire case theory that the Prosecution argued at different stages of the trial. To illustrate this, let me recall that in their pre-trial brief the Prosecution do not say that the police was resubordinated to the army; rather, they insist on co-ordination between the army and the police. Then, at trial, the Prosecution argued, as did their experts, that there were cases of resubordination but that they were relatively rare. Next, they argued that there was a difference between resubordination and co-ordinated action. Subsequently, they held that resubordination was carried out solely in the course of combat and not otherwise in other actions. Two days ago, we heard yet another version because at page 27340 of the transcript, in reference to P624 and the percentage of the MUP members who were resubordinated, Ms. Korner said: "Clearly the document says that they participated in combat but it does not say that they were resubordinated in these actions." On the other hand, yesterday, Mr. Olmsted said that MUP members were resubordinated whilst on the front in combat. Laterally, they argued that even when resubordinated the police retained the capacity of authorised officials. They also continued having effective control over their members and had the right and obligation to enforce discipline and run criminal investigations. The same applies to the Prosecution final brief. Here, again, we have various alterations. Although in the opening statement I highlighted the fact that the Prosecution completely misrepresented the context of the events in 1992, and although I noted with concern the extent to which the Prosecution exhibited a lack of familiarity with the legal system and regulations of the former SFRY and BH, nevertheless, throughout the case, the Prosecution chose to ignore these issues and the same is true of their final brief. As an English philosopher and historian Sir Isaiah Berlin would put it, history is not only what happened but what happened in the context of what could have happened. Clearly the Prosecution do not espouse this line of thinking, which is very true, because their view of history is monochrome and superficial. Let me remind you of some of the changes that the Prosecution went through during their case. From the start of trial, the Prosecution withdrew 91 witnesses and added 74 others. They had 2.061 documents on their 65 ter list, 509 of which were never presented, but 986 others were added. During the Defence case [as interpreted], the Prosecution -- my apologies. I'm sorry, I didn't say "during the Defence case." Some of the crucial documents were disclosed and tendered into evidence during the Defence case without having shown them to their own experts or the numerous witnesses who testified precisely to these circumstances, and I'm referring to P2320, P2339; next, documents shown to Kovacevic and Lisica but not to their OTP military expert. The OTP tendered a number of documents into evidence without having ever disclosed them to the Defence previously. Despite our objections, in most of these cases the Trial Chamber granted these applications and admitted the documents into evidence. We did not press the matter because we understand the position of the Trial Chamber as being that the Prosecution have the duty to prove matters beyond a reasonable doubt, a standard that is higher than the one that the Defence has to meet. However, there are several glaring examples that I will come back to later which, in our view, have an impact on the integrity of the proceedings. Let me also remind you that in relation to the CHS, the Prosecution tendered six different versions of documents as a result of the objections and omissions raised by the Defence. They continued modifying and adding documents into the so-called database even -- not only after the end of their case but even after both Defence cases ended on the 5th of April this year. Specifically, in that group of documents supposedly supporting the victim database and among the documents that are alleged intercepts, there is a large number of documents that were admitted, in our view, in violation of Rule 95 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the ICTY jurisprudence. I am sure that you will remember, Your Honours, how many times the Prosecution challenged the authenticity of certain documents of the Defence only to establish subsequently that they, too, were in possession of these documents, but that, apparently due to difficulties in conducting searches, they were unable to identify them. There were also cases where suggestions were made, although not directly, that the Defence had put some sort of pressure on witnesses or contacted them before their testimony, all of which proved incorrect. Your Honours, this was just a short summary overview of the procedure, and I would like the Trial Chamber to note that there is an identical pattern of conduct that can be observed in the Prosecution final trial brief. I must say that the final trial brief of the Prosecution came as a major surprise to me three years into the trial and after all the evidence adduced, because most of what we were able to hear and read at trial was simply ignored. At first glance, the Prosecution brief appears to be a coherent document with a great many references, but that is the case only at first glance, since there is a considerable number of cases where the reference given does not correspond to the conclusion drawn in the paragraph involved. In some cases, it is probably an error; in other, it is evidence misconstrued; still others, erroneous interpretation. There is a considerable number of paragraphs where evidence as a whole is completely ignored or disregarded or construed in a way that doesn't have any foundation or there are paragraphs where all these elements appear combined. The impression gained from reading the Prosecution final trial brief is that the events seem to have happened in a vacuum as there is no mention of a cause and effect relationship between the various events. The events appear to be unfolding, according to the Prosecution, without any context whatsoever, especially perilous are the following examples that I urge the Trial Chamber to pay special attention to. It is only natural, given the nature of this procedure, that on account of interpretation or a confusing question, a witness would misunderstand the question put to him. As a result, when reading the witness's entire evidence, one can tell that at some points the witness said something that was quite the opposite of everything he had been claiming all along. I think that Ms. Korner spoke of that yesterday. I think it is inappropriate on the part of the Prosecution to quote precisely these portions of evidence where it is obvious that the witness concerned misunderstood an issue. For this reason, I would like the Trial Chamber to pay special attention to such cases that I will specifically refer to in the course of my closing arguments and to consider when assessing the evidence as a whole the testimony in its entirety and not the one lone sense quoted by the Prosecution. From the very start of the Prosecution brief introduction there are several examples of the OTP's lack of consistency that I will stress. At paragraph 2, the Prosecution argues that the police was the only organised armed force in Republika Srpska at the very start. Here, the Prosecution exclude the Territorial Defence. Although in their pre-trial brief at paragraphs 96 and 105, they argued that the police together with the TO was the only armed formation. It is a fact that during the Prosecution case a significant amount of evidence was adduced about the existence, functioning and arming of the TO even before the RS MUP came into being. At paragraph 4 of the final brief, the Prosecution were commenting on the position of the Defence that the Crisis Staffs had an impact on the functioning of the RS MUP and said, “Such statements are easy to make in the absence of accused persons who were members of these bodies.” This comes as a surprise in view of the fact that in this courtroom we heard dozens of witnesses who were members of various crisis Staffs as well as members of the RS MUP who were Crisis Staff members ex officio. In that same paragraph, Prosecution go on to explain that there is overwhelming evidence which indicates that they all had a common goal. They argue that everything was bent on furthering the alleged criminal plan, although all the witnesses claimed that the common goal was to defend the country which is only logical and is a paramount goal of any country. Yesterday and the day before yesterday, at pages 10 and 11 of yesterday's transcript, a similar baseless statement was reiterated. The Prosecution said that the Defence had the advantage of being able to shift the blame on the deceased, specifically Todorovic and Drljaca, and the Prosecution were evidently oblivious to the fact that they, themselves, sought the admission of portions of Todorovic's testimony, pursuant to Rule 92 quater, and this is something the Defence subsequently did in respect of other portions of testimony. Likewise, it was the Prosecution that -- who, for the most part, sought the admission of the documentation related to Simo Drljaca. On the issue of Stanisic's interview, I refer you to what the Prosecution had to say at paragraphs 10 to 12; whereas, the paragraphs of our brief dealing with this issue are 15 to 17. The Prosecution suggest that the Trial Chamber should trust only Stanisic's incriminating statements and not the rest. This statement by the Prosecution escapes comprehension especially in view of the fact that it was the Prosecution who sought the admission of Stanisic's interview and not the Defence, and as I said yesterday it was done through a bar table motion. They relied entirely on that document for the truthfulness of its contents, as was the case with all the other documents included in the bar table motion. This is an example of a striking lack of consistency on the part of the Prosecution because the bar table motion does not contain any sort of submissions of the kind that were set out in the final brief. If the Prosecution had any sort of reservations as to the truthfulness of this document, then, by the very nature of things, they would not have sought its admission or relied upon it. The Prosecution team, led by the experienced lawyer, Mr. Tieger, interviewed Stanisic over the course of five days showing him documents and asking that he answer questions. He answered questions and explained the contents of various documents and why they were written, and he said that all of his answers, as well as the entire contents of the interview, can be used at trial. This is something that the Prosecution ultimately did, and at paragraph 15 of our brief, we say what the bar table motion had to say about this interview. Also, at paragraph 16 of our brief and footnote 22, we cite examples where the Prosecution, clearly relying on this interview in their pre-trial brief, in the opening statement, and in the course of trial, spoke of this. Yesterday, Ms. Korner cited the interview and read certain portions of it, only to say at the end that they were not relying on that interview. Your Honour, I am aware of the fact that my knowledge of the adversarial procedure and principles is very limited, and I offer my apologies. However, I believe that one of the principles that should stand is that the Defence should be put on notice of the nature of the Prosecution case, and that it is on this basis that the Defence would be able to build their case. If the Prosecution continue to rely on a piece of evidence throughout only to say at the very end that they would no longer be relying on it, I don't see how the Defence would in that case be able to answer the Prosecution case. In that way, the Defence would, in fact, be mislead. A small aside, yesterday, when I quoted the jurisprudence of the Tribunal on this issue and similar issues, I neglected to underline that in all the three cases that I cited, the Milutinovic et al, Perisic and Popovic et al cases, the interviews with the accused and the OTP were introduced as Prosecution exhibits. In two of these cases it was done identically as in this case, i.e., through a bar table motion, and in Popovic through a Prosecution investigator who interviewed the accused. The next example I want to refer you to is in paragraph 13 of the final trial brief of the Prosecution and relates to the so-called insider witnesses. Let me remind you -- let me remind you that in the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution -- at paragraph 18, the Prosecution argued that, and I quote: "The testimony of these witnesses would allow the Trial Chamber to clearly see the joint criminal enterprise charged by the Prosecution, its goals and methods, its members, and the role of the accused in the joint criminal enterprise." As you know full well, their testimonies, in fact, confirmed quite the opposite. Yet again, the Prosecution insinuate, in a manner that I have to say is highly improper, that the reason why witnesses allegedly changed their previous statements was the discussions they had with the Defence before that testimony. If such an insinuation was not inaccurate, unfair and unbefitting of fellow members of the profession, I would consider it a true compliment. The ability to use 30 minutes to meet with a witness for the first time and managed to persuade him to change his testimony would, indeed, amount to a supreme skill. Furthermore, the Prosecution suggest that when assessing the probative value and weight of these testimonies, the Trial Chamber should bear in mind a number of factors, among others, the motive for giving false testimony. Such a patently inaccurate statement requires some attention. In fact, the Prosecution engages in an impermissible speculation in this case in view of the facts. The Prosecution are oblivious to the fact that although Trial Chamber repeatedly called on them to disclose previous statements or interviews of the viva voce witness, the OTP refused to do so, unlike the Defence who disclosed all the interviews and statements of Defence witnesses to both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. What is more, we even suggested that the OTP interviews of Defence witnesses be admitted into evidence under Rule 92 ter, an application that the Trial Chamber denied. According, Your Honour, the interviews that the Prosecution claim contain these inconsistencies in witness statements are not before you at all. So, in fact, you should, if I may put it that way, make a leap of faith and trust the Prosecution when they say that there are inconsistencies and formulate your opinion of the value of their testimonies accordingly. Let me recall that in the cases where the Prosecution showed their witnesses the previous interviews, the witnesses gave clear and compelling reasons and explanations accounting for certain discrepancies in their answers. In fact, the very fact that the witnesses -- that there are inconsistencies in their statements is an indication that they tell the truth as established by the ICTY jurisprudence in some earlier cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Although the interpreters have not indicated they have a problem, I suspect that you are going a bit too fast, so please bear in mind that you have to be interpreted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'm sorry -- I apologise to the interpreters if I am rushing. I will keep a slower pace. [Interpretation] As far as I recall, there was only one case where the Prosecution asked that one of their witnesses be declared a hostile witness. To the best of my recollection, at no point during the trial did they suggest that any of their witnesses were providing a false testimony. This speaks volumes about how founded this OTP position is. The Prosecution spoke about this yesterday at page 10 of the transcript and reiterated their position from the final brief. I do not agree with the assertion that the witnesses considerably changed their statements. In my view, it was the case of the Prosecution teams who interviewed them who were either not prepared sufficiently for these interviews, or, for reasons known to them alone, failed to put crucial questions or address material facts. The Trial Chamber should always bear in mind that under such circumstances, the statements of all these witnesses have to be interpreted or translated and then they become documents. Let me remind you of the case of Witness ST-187 who testified as a 92 ter witness. The Defence interviewed the witness and it did so several days before he took the stand because the Prosecution insisted that we do it that way in order for them to have an opportunity to additionally proof the witness for his testimony. In his testimony in the Krajisnik case, the witness said that he was ordered to send the dispatch of the 31st of March, 1992, which is P353, by Stanisic. The Defence questioned the witness about this fact, and he reneged it, and he testified as much in your presence, Your Honour. The Prosecution clearly knew the Defence would be challenging this portion of his testimony from the Krajisnik case because Stanisic himself denied it in his interview. Instead, what happened, the night before the witness was to appear, the proofing note did not contain a single word about this particular change and the Defence counsel sent an e-mail to the Prosecution -- was sent on this new development. And I'm sure you remember that on the following day we had lengthy discussions about it in court. However the gist of the matter is as follows: The Prosecution never asked the witness to confirm this fact although they knew that he spoke to the Defence and that it could be expected that the Defence would be questioning him about it. This is a perfect example of the selective approach adopted by the Prosecution which I believe is evident throughout this case. The Prosecution developed a case theory suited to their own needs, rather than the underlying evidence, and every interview that was conducted with witnesses was aimed solely at confirming facts from that imagined theory rather than eliciting credible information. This is quite evident and can be readily seen in the contents of the final trial brief of the Prosecution. What poses a veritable problem for the Prosecution is the fact that all these so-called insider witnesses were compelling. Their testimonies were consistent with those of other witnesses who testified to the same issues, and, more importantly, they were fully consistent with the evidence both of the Prosecution and the Defence, with orders, minutes from meetings and contemporaneous reports. That is the only reason why at present the Prosecution is asking that you, Your Honours, trust their witnesses in cases where it suits the OTP theory and to mistrust them where that is not the case. In their final brief, the Defence explicitly cited the portions of testimonies of specific witnesses that cannot be accepted and substantiated it with reasoning and evidence. We are convinced that the Trial Chamber will, as stated on a number of occasions, assess the totality of evidence and base their conclusions on that. We also believe that the evidence can only be assessed in its entirety and we seek that the testimony of these witnesses be assessed in correlation with the evidence and testimonies of other witnesses on the same issues. After all, it was the Prosecution who chose the witnesses to call in their case and to base their case theory on. If they had any reason to doubt the veracity of statements of these individuals who are now being represented as alleged members -- as members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, then they should not have called them to begin with. Now that we're on this issue, I'm sure that the Trial Chamber also observed that the Prosecution did not call a single witness from the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a Muslim, to possibly refute the facts that Stanisic related in his interview. In the course of his interview Stanisic stated who were the colleagues from the former MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina he spoke to, what they spoke about, and when. At least several of them were mentioned during the interview, and they were mentioned countless times during trial: Delimustafic, Hilmo Selimovic, Mr. Pusina, Kemal Sabovic, Avdo Hebib. As far as I know, all of these witnesses are alive and well and within easy reach of the OTP. These witnesses could easily have testified to the facts related to Stanisic's character, his alleged connections with the SDS, his alleged membership of the JCE, the MUP -- the split in the MUP, and other facts on which the Prosecution built their case. At any rate, the Prosecution would not have had to, instead, prove their points with evidence that had significantly less weight by interpreting their probable contents. Nevertheless, the Prosecution never invited any one of them, and chose to introduce Stanisic's interview as evidence. Yesterday, or, was it the day before, that Ms. Korner said at page 42, that for obvious reasons you were unable to hear the testimony of any of the members who were Muslims, members of the MUP BH. I don't see why that would be so obvious. The only reasonable explanation for such a position would be that in their contacts with the OTP, these individuals confirmed what Stanisic said in his interview, and the Prosecution did not call them because their testimonies confirming Stanisic's interview would probably have fatal consequences for the Prosecution case. I suppose that was the only reason why they chose to call the so-called insider witnesses so that in the event that their testimony did not suit them they could suggest that the Trial Chamber should reject their testimonies in their entirety. After all, this is what they did in their final brief and what they reiterated in their closing arguments. I will remind the Trial Chamber that several of the witnesses called by the Defence were originally on the Prosecution list but were subsequently withdrawn by the Prosecution. Let us now move to the contents of the Prosecution final brief. As follow-up to what I said so far, I will cite several examples of the lack of consistency on the part of the Prosecution when it comes to what they say in their final brief and the evidence that they adduced or their misinterpretation in relation to the JCE. On the issue of the JCE, at paragraphs 14 to 51, the Prosecution speak about a clear pattern of conduct and the Defence deals with these issues at paragraphs 89 to 97 of our final brief. Obviously all these various occurrences that the Prosecution lists are viewed in full isolation and outside of the context of the events in the former SFRY. Once the right to self-determination was recognised to the peoples in the Republic of Croatia, Slovenia and Macedonia, under that same principle, these rights had to be guaranteed to the other peoples including the Muslims, Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The gist of it is that there are reasons that are of a completely different nature but that are equally rational and valid. There are other causes of these events that need not necessarily be related to any sort of criminal plan. Therefore, regional associations were created such as the ARK or Herceg-Bosna which was created by the Croatian people at more or less the same time in a manner that was quite legitimate and in accordance with the constitution and laws. The Muslims were in favour of a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina and did not create regional associations. Certain Serb regional associations such as northern Bosnia have never really become operational, and this is something the Prosecution did not dispute. Therefore, to assert that regionalisation is part of the plan is something that is untenable. How can one account for at least two facts that are contradictory? Namely, that the Croats themselves were creating an identical association at the same time and they were definitely not a part of the plan, and the fact that some of the Serb regional associations that were allegedly so important to the plan were not established at all or did not become operational. Similarly, the creation of parallel structures need not be related in any way with the alleged plan. The evidence in the case file indicates that this was a direct result of the violation of the constitution committed to the detriment of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the formation of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the subsequent plebescite were a democratic responses on the part of one ethnicity to the fact that their legitimate rights were denied as testified to by a number of witnesses cited in paragraphs 93 and -- to 97 of our final brief. Propaganda and a climate of fear are tools employed by all the media regardless of the ethnicity they belonged to and invariably directed against members of other ethnicities and that trend unfortunately emerged as early as in 1990, with the emergence of national parties throughout the SFRY, and therefore this need not be the only logical explanation that that was the part of an alleged plan. I don't want to delve into an in depth analysis of the strategic goals which are mentioned by the Prosecution at least in three places in the final brief. I'm just going to present the facts which clearly show that the conclusion by the Prosecution is not the only rational explanation; namely, those strategic goals were defined for the first time in mid-May 1992 when the war had already started. The list of those goals was only published in 1993 and then that list became an official document when it was published in the Official Gazette. In the Prosecutor's reference with paragraph 43 it is stated or, rather, one part of the Karadzic's speech is quoted and in that speech he defined the goals and that speech was taken out of the context because Karadzic says in there that the strategic goal of the SDS was a three-partite Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that that goal had already been achieved because it had been accepted by the European Union, by the international community, by Cutileiro's agreement and this is a fact. Strategic goal number 1 is quoted by the Prosecution in its incomplete form because it omits to mention the word state. In the speech, it is referred to the state separation from the other two people, i.e., the creation of institutions in all of the three entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, I believe, was a legitimate right of the Croatian and Serbian peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were entitled to taking their destiny into their own hands after the violation of the constitution at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in October and December 1991. In paragraphs 52 to 62, the Prosecution speak or provides the background for the creation of the RS MUP and the Defence deals with these issues in paragraphs 44 through 88 and 98 through 161 of their final brief. Again, there is a very reasonable and very rational explanation for the creation of the RS MUP which doesn't have to do -- anything with the joint criminal plan. Namely, if a tripartite federation was created based on negotiations and an agreement with the support of the European Union, and if the entities were given the right to form certain bodies, including the Ministry of Interior within such an organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then embarking on that was part of a legitimate process which had been agreed. The Dayton Agreement which was signed in 1995 provided for the identical organisation which still exists. I'm sure that the Prosecution do not want to apply the same standard to the Dayton Accord and they don't want to put Dayton Accord into the context of the JCE. In light of what the Prosecution said yesterday about the plan of the division of the MUP, I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that the international community had started negotiating with the warring parties in the former SFRY already in the summer of 1991 and that the negotiations about the future organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina started in September 1991 at the latest; and, after that, Badinter's Commission started making conclusions from 1991. In other words, Cutileiro Plan and Lisbon agreements were actually only the end of the process which was launched at least six months before that under the auspices of the international community. Moreover, in paragraphs 63 to 68, the Prosecutor speaks about the members of the criminal enterprise and provides conclusions without any references in the footnotes; i.e., based on the same sort of understanding and theory which the Prosecutor himself built without relying on any evidence, on any piece of the evidence of 4.500, or the transcript pages of over 27.000 pages. The day before yesterday, Mr. Demirdjian said on page 14 that the JNA systematically distributed weapons via the SDS within the framework of a well-orchestrated plan. However, on page 54 on the same day, Ms. Korner said that even before the Army of Republika Srpska had been established on the 12th of May, the MUP was the only armed force on which the Bosnian Serbs could rely at the moment because they didn't know whether the JNA would help them, whether the JNA would place themselves on their side in case of conflict. The way I see it is the claim that the JNA was not part of the plan, so I'm no longer sure what the position of the Prosecution is on this issue. In the part of the Prosecution brief entitled: Implementation of the alleged plan, paragraph 69 through 85, I believe that one should remember the findings of the Trial Chamber in the Galic case as a preliminary legal issue. In paragraph 199, it was established that the armed conflict started on the 6th of April, 1992, which is also the date that the war crimes Tribunal in Bosnia and Herzegovina accepts in its decisions; for example, designation number X-KR-05/58 and the appeals decision X-KRZ-05/58. In paragraphs 82 and 83 of their final brief, the Prosecution speaks about the reports on the war victims by expert Ewa Tabeau and the claim on the number of victims among civilians and soldiers. I believe that the -- these claims have not been documented and cannot be relied on in view of the serious faults of the CHS document that we came across. It is indicative that the expert, Mrs. Tabeau, which is also an employee of the Prosecution, did not have an opportunity to take a critical stance and evaluate the accuracy of the information of the so-called victims database of the Prosecution. When it comes to the Prosecutor's final brief where the Prosecutor deals with the implementation of the alleged plan in municipalities, I will just provide a brief comment on those municipalities which are not covered by the Zupljanin indictment because I believe that the Zupljanin Defence will deal with that in quite detail. Let me start by saying that there's no proof, that there's no order by the RS MUP on any activity regarding the take-over of municipalities. If the statement were -- by the Prosecution were correct that the MUP was a hierarchical structure and that allegedly there was a clear pattern of conduct with regard to the take-over of municipalities, how is it then possible that there is no single order or instruction by the RS MUP in that regard? Your Honours, the first municipality that the Prosecutor deal -- deals with is Pale, and you saw from the evidence that Pale is one of the municipalities of the city of Sarajevo. During the proceedings, it was established that a lot of Serbs fearing the situation in Sarajevo fled Sarajevo and ended in Pale. Koroman was the chief of the SJB and he was appointed by Minister Delimustafic. It is a fact. You also heard evidence and testimonies that the take-over -- the police station at Pale was part -- or, rather, response to the situation at the SJB in Stari Grad from where Chief Jahic expelled Serbs from the SJB, and all that happened before the MUP of the Republika Srpska was even established. In paragraph 104 which deals with the 400 people from Bratunac which were brought to Pale, the allegations in this paragraph were refuted by the testimony of another Prosecutor's witness, which was explained in paragraph 500 of our final brief. Paragraphs 109 to 124 of the final brief of the Prosecution deal with the municipality of Bijeljina. The Defence brief deals with these issues in paragraphs 487 through 494. Also, in paragraph 114, it is -- the statement in that paragraph is not founded, since Jesuric was appointed chief of the SJB, or, rather, reappointed again by Minister Delimustafic, and then from the position as the chief of the SJB he became the chief of the CSB in the MUP of Republika Srpska. P1409 speaks about the temporary appointment, starting with the 1st of April, whereas the appointment of the 15th of May is related to an order which was issued on the 15th of May. And it is incorrect that that appointment was permanent. We are explaining that in detail in our brief in paragraphs 205 and 206. The fact is that Jesuric was soon removed from that position and the Prosecutor does not challenge that fact. Please look at P876. In paragraph 116, dealing with the murders of Muslims in Bijeljina and the murder of Muslims and families by Dusko Malovic in September, the allegations are incorrect. If we look at what Witness Adnan stated, and please look at document 1D97, we explain our position in our brief in paragraphs 332 through 333 and 338 through 384. I will re-visit this issue later. And now onto paragraphs 117 through 119, where the Prosecutor deals with Batkovic camp. Your Honour, the police had nothing whatsoever to do with Batkovic camp. It -- they did not have authority. They did not have the any knowledge about that. Witness Adnan testified about that and there is also evidence 1D730 that specifically confirms that. We deal with this issue in our paragraphs 503 through 506 in our final brief. The adduced evidence also confirmed that it was the police that liberated Muslims from Mauzer's detention and arrested Mauzers and we speak about that in paragraph 343 of our final briefly. In paragraphs 136 through 144 the Prosecutor deals with Manjaca. The Defence deals with these issues in paragraphs 503 through 506. Your Honours, numerous reports about the work and the interviews of military investigators in Manjaca were submitted to the military security bodies. None of them were ever submitted to the MUP, and this all arises from the evidence listed in footnote 988 of our final brief. When it comes to Zvornik, the municipality of Zvornik, the Prosecutor deals with that in paragraphs 145 through 156, and the Defence deals with these issues in paragraphs 331, 472 through 486, 351 through 365, and 597. And now onto Visegrad. The Defence deals with the issues of Visegrad in paragraphs 373 and 469 of our final brief. The Defence deals with the issues of Gacko in paragraphs 466 through 471, and 517 of our final brief. When it comes to Visegrad, I would like to say that the Prosecutor deals with the take-over of Visegrad and that the Prosecution's allegations are a fabrication. The fact is that Visegrad was taken over by the JNA and that there was a clear military need to do that. Namely, several individuals occupied the dam and they threatened that they would open the dam and all the settlements downstream of the Drina river would be flooded. In paragraph 182 of the Prosecutor’s brief, the allegations about the Obrenovac detachment are incorrect. Obrenovac, Your Honours, is a city in Serbia, some 30 kilometres away from Belgrade. Indeed, Milan Lukic was a policeman there but he was a member of the MUP of Serbia and the RS MUP did not have any authority whatsoever over its members. For that reason, that group was attached to the paramilitary group White Eagles as the Prosecution alleged. Yesterday on page 50, Mr. Olmsted quoted Witness ST-79 and confirmed precisely what I have just stated. Paragraph 186 in the Prosecutor's brief contains an allegation -- a conclusion, according to which a report by Chief Perisic which was submitted directly to the RS MUP, and it says in that report that the police expressed a lack of professionalism. They're referring to P633. I believe that this is very indicative and that it confirms the assertions of the Defence. It is clear from the text that this is actually the first report that was ever sent to the RS MUP from Visegrad. It was sent in mid-July, to be more precise, on the 13 July. It was sent by courier which means that there were no other means of communication. And this document confirms that the local authorities appointed the leading personnel of the SJB and it says furthermore that there were only five active police officers there. That document also points to some serious problems that the SJB had with paramilitary groups. In paragraphs 368 through 373 of our final brief, we list all the measures that were undertaken by Stanisic and the RS MUP with regard to that part of Republika Srpska. In the following paragraphs, namely, 188 through 210, the Prosecutor deals with Bosanski Samac. The Defence deals with those issues in paragraphs 492 through 453, 578 through 579, and 614 through 622. Two days ago, Mr. Demirdjian, on page 27307 of the transcript, spoke about mass killings, and he mentioned the murder of 80 people in Crkvine. A decision of this Tribunal in the Simic et al case for crimes committed in Bosanski Samac, where I happened to be counsel so I'm very familiar with the case and the decision, in that decision, in paragraph 358, it is established that a total of 16 people were killed in Crkvine. The indictment in this case, Annex 10.1, charges the murder of 18 people in Crkvine. I suppose that the Prosecutor misspoke or that he made an unintentional mistake in the number. Paragraphs 228 through 250 deals -- deal with the municipality of Vlasenica. The allegations proffered in these paragraphs do not correspond to the contents of the evidence. During the proceedings, Your Honours, it was established, and ST-179 testified about that, that he was appointed only on the 8th of August, 1992, as the chief of the SJB. The fact is that before the 15th of May he never even set foot in the public security station building because it had been attacked and taken over by paramilitary formations. When he arrived he found a special attachment there as well as a reservists' detachment. The allegation in paragraph 228 according to which the chief could report to his superiors in the CSB Sarajevo and the RS MUP about what was going on in their municipality, including the massacre in Drum and the beating at the SJB is absolutely incorrect. The evidence referred to by the Prosecutor testified to quite the opposite. ST-179 testified that he had started to reporting to the -- his superiors only after he was appointed on the 8th of August, 1992, which means nearly four months from the start of the hostilities in the municipality. The allegation presented in paragraph 236 of the Prosecutor's brief where it says that when he was pressed, ST-179 agreed that the police detachment that he had found there had been established pursuant to Stanisic's order of 15 May. But this is incorrect. The witness on several occasions during his testimony stated that that unit had been established by the Crisis Staff, and that pursuant to a decision by the Crisis Staff, it was attached to the SJB which neither him nor Bjelanovic accepted. And that is on transcript page 7458. In paragraph 234, the Prosecution claims on the basis of evidence that that unit was established immediately after that -- after the take-over of Vlasenica, i.e., in April 1992. So it remains, indeed, unclear how come that the Prosecution concluded that it had been established based on the order that was issued on the 15th of May, which did not even exist at the time. It was established one month prior to that order. There is no proof that any information about the crimes committed by this unit was ever sent to the RS MUP. Your Honours, I'm looking at the time. The time is running out. I'm going to skip a few municipalities that have been dealt with in our final brief, and I will speak shortly about the municipality of Brcko. I'm talking about paragraphs 302 through 325, and the relevant paragraphs about -- of our issue are 328 through 330, and 347, 348 and 492 of the Defence brief. In paragraph 315, the Prosecutor claims that Goran Jelisic was a reserve policeman. You will remember, I hope, that during my opening statement I suggested to Ms. Korner that the judgement of this Tribunal in the Jelisic case did not establish that he was a member of the RS MUP. The day before yesterday, Mr. Demirdjian showed some photos from Brcko on page 27308, and he said the policeman killed three civilians in the middle of the street, without stating the name of the policeman. Your Honours, those are notorious photos depicting Goran Jelisic. He documented his crime for posterity and he was convicted by this Tribunal for this crime. It's very hard for me to believe that the Prosecution doesn't know that. However, this is just yet another example how the Prosecution case is built without any context. The Prosecution relied on some lists of the alleged reserve policemen and we don't know who made those list, when they were made. Your Honours, numerous witnesses during the proceedings testified about the general mobilisation and they said that chaos reigned supreme, that everybody who had some clout or knew somebody in the municipality would be put on the lists of the alleged reserve policemen in order to avoid being sent to the front line. This is only logical and understandable. Even the well-known criminals and psychopaths such as Celo, Prazina, on the one side, and, on the other side, Jelisic and Cesic found themselves on such lists. Now, what does that have to do with the MUP of Republika Srpska? Because the MUP of Republika Srpska does not have those lists. The MUP does not even have criminal records of those people because they were destroyed. This is not the kind of evidence that the Trial Chamber can rely on. Another example is paragraph 321 where the Prosecution alleges that the bulletin of the RS MUP of the 6th of May reports that there was fierce fighting going on in Brcko. However, the evidence points that civilians were being killed and not soldiers, and as reference, it states P142. If you look at that piece of evidence, and I kindly ask you to do that, you will see that it only contains a statement that there was fierce fighting going on, and that's all. Furthermore, the Prosecution claims that the MUP ignored and covered up the killings of non-Serbs in the same paragraph. However, Witness Ignjic himself, that the Prosecution refers to, claims that on the order of the chief of police, he performed forensic analysis of the bodies and made records of that, and you will find this in Exhibit P144. He also confirmed that there were investigations of those crimes and you will find that on transcript page 1872. So this is yet another case of incorrect and incomplete presentation of -- over evidence. Paragraph 325 is where the Prosecution claims that Avlijas was told only about 226 bodies, and, furthermore, according to Ignjic's testimony that was an attempt of the SJB Brcko to cover up a mass murder of non-Serbs and that the SJB Brcko did not give him anything with which he could carry out the forensic examination of the victims. This is incorrect. Namely, the evidence speak about the opposite. Namely P393 is indeed Avlijas's report that he drafted in October 1992, and it says in that report that due to the alarming information by the ICRC, that in Brcko there were allegedly 2500 bodies. Avlijas checked the situation and he was able to establish that there were 226 bodies that had been buried and the documentation on the death and identification was kept, and he suggests that the documentation should be submitted to the ICRC and if the international organisation demanded, that exhumation should be carried out. The information about 226 victims which was presented in October 1992 fits in with P146 where Witness Ignjic recorded up to mid-July 1992 a total of 216 bodies. Ignjic was not shown P393 and he never provided any comments on that exhibit. However, the witness confirmed on transcript page 1921 that the forensic examination was not done by the book but that was due to the war. Therefore, the OTP's conclusion that this was an attempt on the part of the SJB Brcko to cover up a mass murder is not correct because it is not corroborated by evidence. Never after that, information about 2500 victims in Brcko was either repeated or verified; i.e., the information was false. Your Honour, I will now skip a few paragraphs, and I will go to page 38. I'm saying this for the benefit of the interpreters. When it comes to the implementation on the regional level, the Prosecution deals with the CSB Sarajevo, and we deal with this issue in our final brief in paragraphs 472 and 476. The allegation presented here about the CSB Sarajevo - this is the Prosecutor's claim - according to which the CSB Sarajevo mostly had good communication with the subordinated SJBs is absolutely incorrect as may be concluded from the overall evidence. This statement arises from the report from October 1992 where it says literally that communication had been established with all SJBs but that was only six months after the beginning of hostilities. I will re-visit this issue when I talk about communications. In paragraphs 555 through 561, the Prosecution says that Crisis Staffs functioned as the co-ordinators of municipal authorities, the SDS, the central republican bodies, and the VRS, the police, and other forces as well. Our detailed explanation on this issue may be found in paragraphs 189 through 196 and 595 through 613. Again, this conclusion is erroneous because the instruction for the work of the Crisis Staffs which was issued by the government, which is P70, puts an explicit ban on ordering the army and the police. Many witnesses, including the prime minister, the deputy prime minister, the War Commissioner asserted that the Crisis Staffs were the biggest problem and an obstacle to the functioning of central authorities and that they did not have any control whatsoever over them. It is for that reason that they were soon to be abolished or rather there was a proposal for their abolishment. When that failed they were transformed into War Presidency. Only ten days later, they were transformed into War Commissions, and for the first time, commissioners were appointed by the president of Republika Srpska. And this all obviously points to the fact that this was done in order to establish control so that the president of Republika Srpska could intervene. Further on in the following paragraphs, the OTP obviously ignores evidence and laws, lists all the decisions of the bodies which they passed in keeping with their constitutional authorities, and the OTP treats them erroneously as one part of the implementation of the plan. For example, in paragraph 559 the Prosecution alleges that a National Council of Defence was the predecessor of the Presidency of Republika Srpska. This is not only absolutely incorrect and arbitrary, but it could have been established beyond any doubt, had the Prosecution taken the trouble to consult at least the Constitution of Republika Srpska, if not the other regulations as well. Within this chapter, as part of the implementation of the plan, the Prosecution mentions the decisions such as the selection of the vice-president of the government, the decision on the establishment of civilian and military courts, and so on and so forth. This suggests that the Republika Srpska was as a result of a -- of a criminal enterprise and not the expression of legitimate needs and interests of the Serbian peoples as was finally confirmed by the international community and the Dayton Accord. Your Honours, as I will be moving on to the criminal liability of the accused, under his participation in the JCE, I suggest that we take the break now, perhaps three minutes early, so that I can continue after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Your Honours rise, I did not interrupt Mr. Zecevic at the time because I take the view that you should wait until there is a break. Your Honour, while a certain amount of hyperbole is to be expected and not to be commented on, Mr. Zecevic this morning said, and I'm just going back to -- I believe it's page 12. Sorry. Yes, Your Honours, it's page 12, line 1: "The Prosecution engages in an impermissible speculation in this case in view of the facts. The Prosecution are oblivious to the fact that although the Trial Chamber repeatedly called on them to disclose previous statements or interviews of the viva voce witnesses, the OTP refused to do so, unlike the Defence who disclosed all the interviews and statements of Defence witnesses to both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber." Leaving aside the true situation, Your Honours, what is being suggested here, that we have deliberately flouted a Trial Chamber order to disclose. We, therefore, ask for chapter and verse, rather than these vague and utterly, we say, impermissible statements. Your Honours, there are another matters I'm not seeking to -- at the moment to apply for rebuttal, but this matter is too important, we say, to leave. So we ask for chapter and verse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in a similar vein, Ms. Korner, when Mr. Zecevic was making those representations, he seemed to be criticising the decisions of the Trial Chamber in terms of the admissibility of certain evidence, and it's something on which the Trial Chamber either would have spoken and made a decision, and therefore the parties are bound by it, or it is -- and/or it is something which they could have sought to appeal and didn't. I was going to intervene but I -- inasmuch as just -- just as with the criticism that you have identified in terms of what the Prosecution would have done, he left that area and didn't return to it, so I said nothing further about it at that point. But in terms of the specific and -- and to use your words, the almost inevitable, although unfortunate, hyperbole which one tends to expect in closing arguments, the Prosecution having challenged this assertion which, of course, is on the record, at some point, I expect that the -- Mr. Zecevic, that you would either support it or withdraw it. So we take the adjournment, to come back at 11.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I continue, I wish to apologise to the Trial Chamber and the OTP and, of course, the interpreters. This was absolutely my mistake because I was too fast. What Ms. Korner said was recorded in this transcript is not at all what I wanted to say. We discussed this during the break, and I would provide an explanation once I conclude my closing statements both to the Trial Chamber and Ms. Korner. I will tell you what I had in mind and I will give you the necessary references. But, in any case, I wish to apologise now both to the Trial Chamber and the OTP because of this misunderstanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the issue of the criminal liability of the accused under JCE, that is to say, the joint criminal enterprise, the Defence deals with these issues in paragraphs 636 through 651 and 664 through 670 of our final brief. In the Prosecution final brief, in paragraphs 601 through 607, the Prosecution deals with the claim that Stanisic contributed to the common plan. We state our arguments in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please repeat the number of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraphs are 27 through 43 of our final brief. The Prosecution claim that Stanisic allegedly provided crucial information from his position in the Sarajevo SUP. There is no reference what information they have in mind. No evidence on any information from the Sarajevo SUP was ever presented; therefore, this claim has no foundation whatsoever. It is certainly true that the Presidency and the president of Republika Srpska could have information from a much higher level, the Ministry of the Interior, such as Zepinic or Mandic; therefore, a higher positioned official than Mico Stanisic. In paragraph 602 of the Prosecution final brief, there is a claim that Mico Stanisic was a member of the SDS, and then that he was supported by Karadzic when he was under investigation for providing weapons to the SJB Pale and Ilidza. The reference for these claims are two intercepts of telephone conversations between Mandic and Karadzic in which Mandic provides information that Mandic informs Karadzic in one part that investigation against Mico Stanisic is unfounded because he was doing everything in accordance with the law, as established. Both the Defence and Mico Stanisic personally claim that he was never a member of the SDS. Once again, there is an inconsistency on part of the Prosecution here. If I understood well Ms. Korner, on page 2743 [as interpreted], yesterday, when she talked about Zupljanin, she said the following: "There is no direct evidence that he was a member of the SDS, as opposed to Stanisic." It is on page 27343. However, yesterday on the closing arguments on page 22 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Hannis said: We believe that he was a member of the SDS. Even if he was not a member of the SDS, he was certainly a sympathiser, an important associate or supporter, in other words, Your Honour, there is no evidence that Mico Stanisic was, indeed, a member. Therefore, this is quite contrary to the claim made in the final brief. We do not dispute that all parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina supported the members of their ethnic groups and their cadres but that was because of nationality rather than because of their political affiliation. After all, the Trial Chamber is well aware of our position with regard to intercepts as evidence which we treat in paragraphs 6 and 48 of our final brief. I will move to page 45. In paragraph 605, it is claimed that Stanisic had a key role in the ethnic split in the MUP, and Karadzic's words are quoted as evidence for this claim. So, Your Honours, I will ask you to look at paragraph 605 of the Prosecution final brief and have a look at Karadzic's words which, as I claim, are unclear. It is not clear whether they referred to Zepinic or to Stanisic, and it is also a fact that no witness testified about this or commented on it. A check-point at Vrace and Grbavica is mentioned there, and it is our position that the claim which the Prosecution makes cannot be founded on this. The situation is the same with the Prosecution conclusion about the document, Variants A and B, because there is really no evidence that Mico Stanisic ever received such a document. The fact that someone wrote several names on the back side of the document, including Stanisic 's name, really does not mean that Stanisic did receive this document. The next Prosecution subtitle is Stanisic participated in the formation of bodies and forces that implemented the forcible take-over of the municipalities. Paragraph 609 contains the claim that during the first two meetings of the ministerial council, it was decided to establish an ethnically divided MUP and this was weeks before the Cutileiro Plan. The references are to the two meetings of the ministerial council in which not a single word was spoken about splitting the Ministry of the Interior. I believe that this is another example of misrepresentation and misquotation of evidence. After all, I recently spoke about the fact that discussions about tripartite Bosnia-Herzegovina had been conducted beginning in September 1991 under the auspices of -- or, rather, with the pressure exerted by the international community. In paragraph 611 of the Prosecution final brief, the claim is made that at a subsequent meeting, and then under brackets, probably late March, Mico Stanisic instructed leading member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP to disobey any orders issued by their superiors if they are of Muslim ethnicity and if they were contrary to the interests of the Serbian people. The reference given there is the testimony of Witness Scekic, and the reference given for this claim is transcript page 6528 through 6529. However, this is another instances of misquotation of the contents of the witness's evidence. Namely, the witness discusses this meeting on the following pages of the transcript: 6528 through to 6533, and then 6572 and 6573, and then again answering the questions by the Trial Chamber on page 6587, and, finally, on pages 6590 and 6592. Once you read all the relevant sections of the transcript, you can see that his testimony is the following: That the meeting was most probably held in early April, that it was chaired by Dragan Kijac, it was a brief meeting, and Dragan Kijac was the one who informed those present rather than Mico Stanisic. The witness also said that he is not certain whether Mico Stanisic was introduced at the meeting as the future minister of the MUP of Republika Srpska or as the person who was already the minister. So even in this case, in our view, the contents of the testimony is misrepresented and misquoted. In paragraph 613 of the Prosecution's final brief, it is claimed that the barricades set up on the 1st of March were apparently an attempt to disrupt the pending referendum. Let me just mention one fact here. I thought that it was not in dispute because taking into account the exhibits in this case, the referendum was held as early as on the 29th of February. Therefore, the claim that the barricades were an attempt to disrupt it are unfounded. After all, we have heard what the reasons were, and this is all contained in the exhibits. I mean, the reasons for setting up the barricades. And just to mention this for the sake of interpreters, I will now move onto page 50. Another claim in the Prosecution final brief is that Stanisic communicated and co-ordinated with the Serbian political leaders. These are paragraphs 627 through to 637. Paragraph 629, the reference given for this claim about alleged communication is an alleged intercept. However, once this document is analysed, one can see that this is a transcript made by someone who took notes for a while, noting what the persons engaged in the conversation said, and then the person noting it all provides his own comments and then continues quoting what the interlocutors originally said. Inter alia, it is evident from the contents that Mico Stanisic complained because Mr. Koljevic, who was a member of the Presidency, interfered or, rather, publicly said something that was confidential in connection with an investigation that was conducted by the ministry. Your Honours, it is normal, I believe, and cannot be considered an element of the JCE or anything similar if the minister of the interior is called by the prime minister or members of the Presidency. It is a fact that at that time Stanisic holds a public office and he cannot, in any way, avoid being called by someone on the telephone. The further claim that he was connected with paramilitaries with a reference to the testimony of once of the witnesses is, once again, erroneous, if you take into account the totality of this witness's testimony. Namely, the witness confirmed that he received this information from General Mladic and that therefore he had no direct knowledge. We deal with this issue in our brief in paragraphs 334 through to 350. Answering to Prosecution questions, the witness then claimed that Mico Stanisic gave him carte blanche to take legal measures against all paramilitaries and arrest them. Asked specifically about Arkan, the witness insisted that Mico Stanisic had never told him not to arrest Arkan or anyone else, and that he would have done this with pleasure if he had had the chance. This is on transcript pages 13625 and 13626. After all, Your Honours, there is even not a single piece of evidence that Arkan was present in Sarajevo in 1992 in the first place. For the needs of interpreters, I will now move to page 53. The claims contained in the Prosecution final brief in paragraphs 646 through to 648, I believe that Stanisic made it possible to facilitate the establishment and operation of detention facilities where non-Serb detainees were mistreated and killed. We deal with this issue in paragraphs 511 through to 516 of our final brief. As for the claim that Stanisic was aware of and supported the role of the police in establishing and operating detention facilities at which non-Serbs were held, which is contained in the Prosecution final brief, paragraphs 649 through to 660, I will just comment on this. I already said that we deal with this issue in specific paragraphs of our final brief. I have given you the reference. But the claim contained in paragraph 650, once again, in our view, represents a misinterpretation of evidence. There is, again, a reference to an intercept, and we already noted our position with regard to intercepts and their value. However, the Prosecution claims, based on the transcript of the intercept, cannot be accepted as they are a product of the Prosecution's selective interpretation. Namely, from the transcript of the document P1115, we cannot conclude with certainty what the word "fine" refers to in either instance which the Prosecution quotes. Namely, the word "fine" can be a mere speech filler without any actual meaning or confirmation that he can hear his interlocutor, rather than an expression of his approval. After all, Your Honours, when I reviewed the document, believe me, I established that a reply consisting of the word "fine" is repeat 24 times throughout this document, including contexts which certainly could not denote approval because they refer to the incursion of Muslim units, and so on and so forth. Let me use this occasion to make a comment. The greatest problem with such evidence is precisely that the meaning can be this or that, and neither of the participants in this conversation testified, providing the actual context of the conversation and what the answers referred to, which leaves room for speculation and for different interpretations. In the Defence view, this is impermissible, and this is why, in our final brief and during the Defence case, in principle, we did not rely on intercepts. After all, during his interview with the Prosecution, the OTP did not confront Mico Stanisic with the -- these intercepts in order to establish the context of this conversation and ask for an explanation of the contents. I will now move on to page 56. The claim related to the same topic, which is contained in paragraph 654, that, clearly, the RS MUP was aware that civilians were detained is, once again, an erroneous conclusion. Namely, the Prosecution claims in this paragraph of its final brief that the awareness followed the collegium meeting held on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade which the Defence does not dispute. However, the Prosecution still claims that such an awareness existed even earlier, that the RS MUP was aware of all these things, and then they link that with instructions which are Exhibit P568, which allegedly confirms such a conclusion of the Prosecution. Later on, in its final brief, the Prosecution does say that the instruction is of a general nature and insufficient. However, it is a fact that the witness who is the author of this document explained in detail the context and the reasons for sending such an instruction. He explained that the reminder of the application of the rules of the international law of war and the strict observation of the law was caused precisely by the existence of an armed conflict in the territory and that no -- that he had no information about detained civilians at the moment. Therefore, once again, the conclusion which the Prosecution has drawn is not founded on evidence. The paragraphs of our final brief in which we deal with this issue are 394 through to 396. Further on, it is claimed that Stanisic aided in the government's cover-up of the detention facilities. The relevant paragraphs of our final brief dealing with this issue are 511 through to 517. In the Prosecution claim in 664 that, allegedly, these orders failed to provide details on how the police were to implement these orders or verify that they complied with them, as a result, non-Serb civilians continued to be held and mistreated, is really completely erroneous. Namely, as we explain in our final brief, and as I will touch on later during my closing arguments, such a conclusion is completely wrong. As far as this issue is concerned, please review the documents 1D563, 1D55, 1D56, and 1D57. On the basis of these exhibits, and, of course, the testimony of witnesses, you will conclude that once he learned about this, Stanisic requested that, in all instances when the police detained persons, they should be immediately released and granted freedom of movement, that the police should immediately stop securing POW camps and collection centres and leave it to the military, because the army was in charge of that. In accordance with that, as we can see from all these exhibits, Mico Stanisic ordered that an investigation be conducted, collection of evidence, and filing of criminal reports. Let me remind you that in one of these documents, 1D57 -- I hope you can have a look at it. 1D57, says the following: "The name of the place where the detention camp" -- Mico Stanisic, that is to say, the RS MUP: "Requests the following: "Regardless of jurisdiction, it is necessary that you provide the following data:" Under 1, "the name of the place." Under 2, "who ordered that the institution in question be established and when." Under 3, "who gave the order for people to be brought to these detention camps, collections centres and prisons." Then, "the number of imprisoned people and the number of persons arrested." I think that this sufficiently tells us what Mico Stanisic was aware of and what the position of the MUP of Republika Srpska about this issue was. Further on, the Prosecution claim that Stanisic failed to take adequate measures to protect the non-Serb population and ensure that crimes committed against them were investigated and prosecuted is something that we deal with in paragraphs 378 through to 380, 388 through to 393, and 664 through to 670 of our final brief. So, due to the short time at my disposal, let me not repeat our arguments now. The Prosecution claim made in paragraphs 671 through to 675 that Stanisic had the duty to act is something that we deal with -- deal with in paragraphs 231 through to 245, and 394 through to 408 of our final brief. However, let me comment on this and specifically paragraph 675 of the Prosecution final brief, in which they claim that there is an obligation to ensure that a transfer of prisoners of war to another agent will not diminish the protection the prisoners are entitled to. The Prosecution claims that Stanisic was responsible, regardless of whether the investment or responsibility was made through a legislative enactment of a superior order or as a result of him finding himself with de facto custody over the detainees. This claim from paragraph 675 is linked also with paragraphs 690 and 664 of the Prosecution final brief. For this position, the Prosecution refers to the Mrksic Appeal Judgement. However, Your Honours, this reference to the Mrksic Appeal Judgement is, firstly, a completely erroneous interpretation of the Judgement. Firstly, the facts in the Mrksic case are completely different. Namely, the accused, to whom this section of the Appeals Judgement refers, was on the site and present while the TO members were mistreating the victims. It is therefore evident that he was aware of the possible consequences of transferring prisoners to such a group, and the Trial Chamber was well aware of this. That was why it found him guilty and sentenced him, which, of course, is not the case here because Stanisic was very far removed. As for this conclusion from the Mrksic Appeal Judgement which the Prosecution refers to, the Appeals Chamber, in paragraph 71 of the Appeal Judgement -- I have to place it into the appropriate context because the Prosecution fails to do so. The Appeal Judgement -- therefore, in paragraph 71 of the Appeal Judgement recalls that both the TO and the JNA were agents within one and the same command structure under the command of the Supreme Defence Council, which is not the case here, because the police was not that. Therefore, this position of the Appeals Chamber evidently relates to agents within one and the same command structure. Further, this position relates to the obligation of one agent to ensure that when transferring prisoners to another agent -- will not diminish the rights that the prisoners are entitled to. In other words, the agent must be aware that the agent receiving the prisoners will observe the rights guaranteed to prisoners. In contrast to the Ovcara case where the military police delivered prisoners of war to a group in which, as the Court established, anarchy and violence reigned which did not have clear command structure within the unit, in this case, police handed over the prisoners to the only organ and agent of the state authorised by law, i.e., the Army of Republika Srpska which, as the police knows, pays special attention in its rules to the protection of prisoners of war. In addition to this, it is not disputed that, at the moment, the MUP of Republika Srpska was aware of the instructions of the Supreme Commander and the Ministry of Defence, about strict observation of the international humanitarian law and specific Geneva Conventions. It is also especially important that regulations, and I mean the Law on Military Courts, gives jurisdiction over POWs only to military judiciary. As for the detainees who do not have the status of POWs but who have been arrested, they are transferred to the Ministry of Justice, which, according to the law, is in charge of holding and detaining prisoners in official penal and correctional facilities and prisons, the operation of which is strictly regulated by the rules, just like the obligations and responsibilities with regard to prisoners. Therefore, in this instance, even if we consider that there is an obligation to ensure that the rights guaranteed to prisoners will be observed by other agents, and I mean the military and the Ministry of Justice, this request has absolutely been met. Further, the Prosecution claims in paragraphs 676 and 683 that Stanisic had the ability to act. The Defence position about these issues is expressed in paragraphs 381 through to 387, 416 through to 427, and 583 through to 594 of our final brief. In paragraph 681 of its final brief, the Prosecution makes a claim which is, again, erroneous. Namely, the Prosecution here claims that Mico Stanisic was -- that a lack of expert staff in the police was the result of his own doing, meaning Mico Stanisic, and that this problem that the MUP of Republika Srpska had was a problem of their own doing. However, once again, this claim is unfounded. The evidence shows, and we give references in the paragraphs which I already mentioned, that Stanisic requested that absolutely everyone should stay and decide voluntarily whether they would remain in the Republika Srpska MUP or not. Let me remind you of a document which is dated the 1st of April, 1992, and these are the minutes from the collegium which deal with this, the agreement which was reached at the collegium of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, precisely with regard to these issues. Further, the obligations which are defined by law, such as the obligation to take the solemn oath certainly cannot be changed by a minister's decision. This is also true about the official insignia of the republic, such as the flag, or the insignia. Really, objectively speaking, this all outside the minister's power. In paragraph 684, there is again an evident error or a misinterpretation of the evidence. In any case, the result is a misquotation in the Prosecution footnote 2417, in which it is claimed that Exhibit P190 dates from November 1992, though it actually bears the date the 19th of July. I will return to this document later on and then I will show this to you. The Prosecution claim made in paragraphs 692 through to 696 of their final brief, namely, that Stanisic focuses his resources on combatting looting of state property of Republika Srpska. This is something that we deal with in our final brief in paragraphs 207 through to 222, and paragraphs 231 through to 245. As the Trial Chamber is well aware of, as this has been established during the case, the Ministry of the Interior deals with all forms of crime, and that is his -- its duty according to the law. Once again, this is a characteristic instance of interpretation by the Prosecution where they interpret evidence outside of any context. Namely, Republika Srpska was established, but, clearly, its fiscal organs did not exist, nor was a financial system in existence. Therefore, the state had no income from taxes or similar levies and it was at war. There was no economic production in Republika Srpska at the time because of the war. The only thing that existed were the factories and the big enterprises which needed to be preserved. It is completely normal that a state has an interest to protect its property of great value, such as the TAS factory and several thousand cars. Document P239 deals with that and the deputy prime minister, Mr. Trbojevic, also testified about this. He even said that for this reason the government established a commission to deal with such issues. Exhibit 1D98 is Djeric's letter, that is to say, the letter of the prime minister, addressed to Mr. Kljajic in which he requests information about looting of state property. Considering the totality of evidence and the fact that in -- many evidence presented before the Trial Chamber, it is stated that the priority in the police work were war crimes. The Prosecution claim that Stanisic focussed on combatting looting of state property is evidently wrong. Mr. Macar, who was a witness, testified that the police work cannot be measured by the time spent on a specific case. After all, as you will see later on, Stanisic's letter to Djeric, which is P190, does not talk about TAS or other instances of the looting of property but only about war crimes. As for the claim that Stanisic focussed his resources on documenting and investigating war crimes against Serbs, which the Prosecution deals with in paragraphs 697 through to 702 of its final brief, I will give you a reference because the Defence explains its arguments in detail in paragraphs 409 through to 415 of our final brief. As for Stanisic's action against the Yellow Wasps, which the Prosecution references in paragraphs 703 to 712 of their final brief, and which the Defence addresses in paragraphs 351 to 365 of our final brief, the totality of the evidence presented at trial in relation to this action is completely disregarded and ignored. In the course of their closing arguments yesterday, the Prosecution addressed this issue, and specifically at pages 62 to 63 of the transcript, Mr. Olmsted followed up on what Mr. Hannis had to say on this issue the day before; i.e., that Witness Macar was not a credible witness, in other words, a Defence witness. Interestingly enough, there was another witness, Witness Andan who testified to this issue and there were a number of Prosecution witnesses who testified the same way Witness Macar did. However, their credibility is not raised. Further, the Prosecution quote Exhibit P403, and they say that the issues of war crimes were not raised, only looting. But evidently the Prosecution forget P1539, a Prosecution Exhibit, and it is a record of the statement made in relation to war crimes. After all, the fact of the matter is, Your Honours, that brothers Vuckovic were indicted and convicted of war crimes as a result of a report and documentation gathered in the course of this particular investigation. The fact that they were convicted in Serbia, and they are -- they are nationals of Serbia, only speaks about the fact that the justice administration, the judiciary, did not function in Republic of Serbia -- in Republika Srpska, which is something that the Defence have advanced as their position throughout and something that Mr. Stanisic himself spoke of in the course of 1992. As for the allegations made at paragraphs 709 and 710 about the alleged reasons behind the action against the Yellow Wasps, I think that Witness ST-179 clearly explained his positions and dilemmas on this issue, on the issue of the related incidents. After all, the evidence demonstrates that Stanisic had been preparing the action against the Yellow Wasps for sometime. You will recall that Zugic of the National Security Service was charged by Stanisic as early as in May to start collecting information and evidence related to the Yellow Wasps. Furthermore, the Prosecution fully disregard the evidence that the special police unit, together with a unit -- detachment of the federal SUP, went to Brcko before going to Zvornik to deal with the paramilitaries there. We have written evidence and we have Mica Davidovic and Dragan Andan and many other witnesses testifying to that effect. After Brcko, they went to Bijeljina on the same business. They clashed with Chetnik units, with Mauzer, and at that point they went to Zvornik.
