They were supposed to go to Foca and Visegrad, but for the reasons known to the Trial Chamber that were told by Witness Andan they were unable to do so because Serbia would not allow them to transit their territory. At the end of the year, that same special unit went to Trebinje, Gacko, Rudo, and Cajnice, in other words, the south-western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on that same business; namely, to arrest, to prevent the activities of, and prosecute these paramilitary units. When it comes to the responsibility under other forms of responsibility -- under other forms of liability, rather, that the Prosecution address in their brief, starting from paragraph 809. I will say this briefly because we deal with the topic in paragraphs 625 to 663 of our final brief. At paragraph 809, the Prosecution say only that the Prosecution proved that Mico Stanisic instigated crimes. The fact of the matter is that instigation is not only addressed, but it isn't even mentioned in any of the other paragraphs of the final brief. Therefore, this conclusion, as was the case with many other Prosecution conclusions, do not relate to facts, to all intents and purposes. When it comes to aiding and abetting, as I said, the issue was addressed in our paragraphs between 652 to 663 so I will not repeat that. Under the issue of superior responsibility, we explained our position in paragraphs 671 to 686 of our final brief. I would like to say a few words about this issue. For interpreters, it's page 67. Where the Prosecution say that the accused had effective control over their subordinates, they substantiate their claim with the following statements: That the accused exercised administrative authority over a highly organised and hierarchical police forces. The position of the Defence on this issue is contained at paragraphs 529 to 537 of our final brief. The other assertion made by the Prosecution on effective control says that the accused had strict control over information. The position of the Defence on this issue was explained in detail in paragraphs 261 to 278, and 279 to 284 of our final brief. The Defence brief provides a detailed analysis of the quality of the existing communications as well as the amount and quality of information reaching the RS MUP. The assertion made by the Prosecution that the system of informing and reporting was satisfactory and operational is simply hard to believe, in view of the totality of evidence which speak to the contrary. Can you please look at slide 5 now. It's a graph that we made on the basis of the testimonies of Witnesses Pejic and Kezunovic, as well as based on Exhibit P265 and 1D338. I believe that the graph clearly shows what the situation was in the relevant period, objectively speaking. The accused had the authority to undertake criminal and disciplinary procedures against subordinates. This assertion was made at paragraphs 860 -- 850 to 862. Now, the position of the Defence is -- is expounded at paragraphs 538 to 563 of our Defence brief. I have to stay with this issue for a while. Give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is beyond dispute that it is the duty of a superior to take necessary and appropriate measures within his power. That would, by the very nature of things, include the initiation of a criminal procedure if the instant case includes criminal responsibility. However, when it comes to superior responsibility within the Ministry of Interior, the situation is quite specific. Such an authority to undertake a criminal investigation or a criminal procedure is vested with all the authorised officials of the Ministry of the Interior who are duty-bound under the law to initiate a procedure as soon as they learn of the perpetration of a crime. This is something that we address in paragraphs 381 to 387 of our final brief. Therefore, this duty, possibility, or authority to file criminal reports, which arises from the law, has no cause-and-effect relationship with their command position or any other post within the hierarchy of the ministry. Since such an authority is vested with a rather large number of individuals, as I say, regardless of their place within the hierarchy, in my view, the question that the case law will have to give an answer to is whether this authority can, in this sense, be considered to be an authority strictly related to superior responsibility or not; of course, within the context of the Ministry of Interior. On the other hand, in view of the fact that there is a wide circles of individuals who are vested with the same authority and in view of the obligation that exists under the law that in every single case they have to exercise this authority and initiate a criminal investigation, the question is: Does a minister have any reasonable basis on which he should doubt that the subordinates within the ministry, authorised officials, are using and exercising this authority in view of the imperative obligation that they have under the law? And I mean these authorised officials. I believe that there is foundation in the position whereby it can be reasonably presumed -- or, rather, that the minister can reasonably presume that his subordinates are exercising this authority because they are duty-bound to do so under the law. In that context, the Prosecution position comes as a surprise to the Defence -- or, rather, their suggestion. Because they seem to suggest that it is the minister of the interior who should be the one to file criminal reports and that would, indeed, in my view, be excessive, in view of the context of the entire situation. Therefore, it is our position that the only thing that can come under command responsibility - and that would be strictly in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs - is the authority to undertake disciplinary procedures and not the authority to undertake a criminal procedure. The assertion made at paragraph 852 of the Prosecution final brief where it is stated that even where a policeman voluntarily resigned from the police on account of a serious disciplinary offence, he is -- he was still subject to disciplinary procedure. This is one of the examples that I drew your attention to at the very start of my submissions today. The Prosecution references this assertion with Witness Rodic. That's transcript T8902 to 8903. However, shortly before the answer quoted here by the Prosecution, this is what Mr. Olmsted asked the witness, and I'll quote it so it will be in English: [In English] "Q. You discussed a couple of issues with regard to -- about the police officer who resigns during the process of disciplinary proceedings, and, therefore, the disciplinary proceedings are cancelled. Do you recall that at the beginning of the session? "A. Yes." [Interpretation] Therefore, not only does the Prosecution in this particular case quote a portion of the testimony that would lead to an erroneous conclusion but also by the very nature of things, the conclusion is pointless. Your Honours, it is not possible to carry out a single disciplinary measure envisaged by the law unless the individual in question is an employee of the police. This because all these disciplinary measures relate to and arise from the individual's employment, such as pay cuts, transfers to a different post, or, as the severest measure under the law, termination of employment with the police. Therefore, if, where a procedure is initiated against an individual, the individual voluntarily resigns from the police, what sense would it make to initiate a procedure? It would be moot and a waste of time and resources. Because the effect that -- the outcome that could be the result of such a procedure has already been achieved through his departure from service. In relation to the positions as stated in the Prosecution final brief at paragraphs 863 to 870 which relate to the assertion that the Crisis Staffs did not diminish the effective control that the accused had, I wish to state that the Defence addressed these issues at paragraphs 595 to 613. The assertion made at 867 reads: "The appointments made by the Crisis Staffs were considered to be the proposals on which the RS MUP -- what the RS MUP considered when making a final determination," and in our view it amounts to the misinterpretation of evidence. The evidence confirms that the local organs were the ones who made appointments within the Ministry of the Interior regardless of what the positions of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska were. They were made completely without the knowledge of the RS MUP and, in some cases, the chiefs that had been appointed by the RS MUP were replaced. You can read more about that in our brief. I do not wish to reiterate our positions, but I do ask Their Honours to read the relevant paragraphs. The last topic before our break will be the assertion that the Army of Republika Srpska did not diminish the effective control of the accused. The Prosecution addressed the matter at paragraphs 871 to 880 of their final brief, and the Defence presented their positions at paragraphs 223 to 230 of our final brief. The most interesting issue here that I would like to mention in my arguments is the issue of the existence of a parallel chain of command, as indicated by the Prosecution at paragraph 639 of the final brief. That's where they mention the issue for the first time. Such a parallel system of command is, in my view, key to proving the existence of other independent authorities who had effective control over RS MUP members. In other words, in support of a position that is the opposite of what the Prosecution contend. Your Honours, if we accept that there is a strict hierarchical structure within the MUP of Republika Srpska, as the Prosecution claim, and if the MUP was, indeed, the way the Prosecution claimed it was, that's to say, a part of a criminal plan, why would it be necessary in that case to form a parallel structure within that same alleged plan, as indicated by the Prosecution? Why would that be necessary? If you have a MUP which is part of a joint -- a common criminal plan and there is a common chain of command, and the Prosecution claim that this sort of MUP is a part of a criminal plan, why would that criminal plan also include a parallel structure? What would be the rationale? What would be the reason for something like that? Your Honours, it is our position that the MUP was not a member of the joint criminal enterprise as a hierarchical structure. According to the evidence, there is an explicit request that the government sent to the Crisis Staffs in its instructions that they should not interfere with the command and control of the army units. And despite such an instruction, the Crisis Staffs were, indeed, in command of the police and the army. This is not in dispute. However, this means that in each and every one of these cases, the Prosecution had their duty and obligation to prove beyond a reasonable doubt which of the two or more order-issuing authorities of the SJB or RS MUP members were, indeed, being obeyed, who -- whose orders were they carrying out, who were they held answerable to, and who did they report to? The evidence adduced at trial, in my view, are evident in that sense. Unfortunately, the priority was indeed with the local authorities, and we did raise this issue more than once in our brief and today. Yesterday, at pages 68 and 69 of the transcript, the Prosecution said, in relation to the principle of the unity of command, where they cited the Strugar Judgement, paragraph 367, something that is obviously misplaced and inapplicable to this situation. However, since it is likely that some of these issues will be discussed on Friday, I will not be spending time on it. All the factors that are familiar to the jurisprudence and which point to the absence of effective control, this is something we discuss at paragraph 677 of our brief, have been proven beyond doubt in this case. The totality of evidence shows that, without a doubt, there were independent authorities who had, without any doubt, effective control over specific RS MUP members. These organs made appointments and replacements of certain individuals, paid them, and gave them orders. In return, these individuals carried out their orders, reported to those organs, and carried out their decisions and regulations. Such organs issued decisions appointing chiefs and even lower-level leaders of public security stations or Security Services Centres. These organs were the ones who changed the territorial jurisdiction of the MUP of Republika Srpska as envisaged by the law. This was in the case of Teslic; the decisions of the Crisis Staff and the municipality to join the ARK Krajina. At times, they would directly change the functional organisation of the MUP of Republika Srpska by subordinating Security Services Centres to the authority of public security stations, as happened in the case of Doboj. All these events, without a doubt, happened independently of the MUP of Republika Srpska and without its knowledge. The evidence shows, beyond doubt, that some of these RS MUP members clearly perceived local authorities as their bosses, rather than the RS MUP, as was the case with Drljaca. This is something witnesses testified to during the instructive visit and this is supported by a number of other exhibits in this case. On the case of Todorovic where the chief of the CSB received threats from the president of the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff, serious threats, when the former asked for his removal; there are many other such examples, and you can find them in the Defence brief. There is a category of individuals who had never become members of the MUP. There was an absence of effective control in that case, in view of the explicit legal regulations. All these categories of individuals did not obey the orders or instructions of the accused. Furthermore, we cited on several occasions during trial examples which show that it is true that members of the RS MUP at the point where they become resubordinated lose the capacity of authorised officials. Whilst they are under the command of a military commander, they cannot exercise the -- the powers vested in them by law because they would highly likely not fall within the scope of the task given to that unit, such as, for instance, manning a firing position, or similar. Therefore, to exercise their powers would be contrary to the order issued by the military commander. On the other hand, if we were to accept the position of the Prosecution, failure to exercise such powers would constitute, under the law, a breach of duty. I suppose, Your Honours, that it is obvious that the theory advanced by the Prosecution is completely untenable. I also wish to say that it was proven beyond doubt that all the witnesses who had leading positions in the RS MUP agree with what I've just said, with the position I've just relayed. They did not consider themselves as superiors to the policemen who were resubordinated. As for the reporting from the subordinates to the accused, the totality of evidence shows that this reporting and informing was not only insufficient in terms of the amount of information available, but the quality of information was unacceptably low, especially in the first six months. There is a considerable number of orders and instructions that the RS MUP was issuing to the lower organs through to the end of 1992. We still have on our screens the graph that I showed you a moment ago. Your Honours, I do think that this is the crucial argument where it comes to the issue of communication. I assert that the issue and the problem of communication was sufficiently addressed and substantiated with the evidence in this case and indicates the permanent nature of this problem that prevailed throughout 1992. Your Honours, I suggest that we take the break now, as I am about to move to a different topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return at 2.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.19 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Your Honours, my next topic for the benefit of the interpreters, I'm on page 76. My next topic, therefore, that I wish to deal with in reference to the Prosecution's brief is the Prosecutor's claim that the accused knew or had reason to know that their subordinated officials committed crimes charged in the indictment. Under 1, it says that the system of reporting in the RS MUP allowed the accused timely access to information about the criminal conduct of subordinated individuals. I have already explained our position at great length. I don't want to go over the same grounds again. I would like to mention for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that we deal with that issue in paragraphs 261 through to 284, and 428 through 494 of our final brief. When it comes to the knowledge and the participation of subordinated individuals in the unlawful detention of non-Serbian population and their ill-treatment, let me say that we deal with this issue in the paragraphs that I have just referred to, but I would also like to provide comment on paragraph 892 of the Prosecutor's final brief. Namely, in paragraph 892 of the Prosecutor's final brief, the Prosecutor claims that Zivko Lazarevic sent regular reports to the National Security Service in Sarajevo about the unlawful detention of civilians in the bunker. A references for this claim is in transcript on page 13009 through page 13015, a total of six pages. However, when you read the testimony in that reference, it is hard to see why this was put on paper. There's no foundation for that. Because what the witness said is literally, I sent my report to Ilidza, and what happened to the report from then on, I don't know. So it is clear that he didn't know that the report was sent to the national security in Sarajevo, and it is also clear that this claim by the Prosecution is founded on misrepresented evidence. In paragraph 938, which refers to the alleged knowledge on the participation of subordinated individuals in the commission of other crimes against non-Serbian population, again, a reference is made to the murder of three Muslim families in Bijeljina. It is stated in here that witness who spoke to Stanisic in the year 2000-and-something, heard from Stanisic that he should not be mentioned in reference to that murder. The Prosecutor spoke about that the day before yesterday in their closing argument. The fact is, Your Honours, that Stanisic provided a statement to the official judicial bodies. That statement is P1543, page 65, and it is in evidence. As the Prosecution also confirms, this murder is not mentioned in the indictment as one of the incidents, and the claim that was done either by Malovic or another member of the MUP of Republika Srpska has not been corroborated. Document P1543 is a complete court file about the event, and that document does not lead to conclusion that either Malovic or the RS MUP platoon from Sokolac were involved in that killing. If there was such evidence, they would have been prosecuted, either Malovic or somebody from that platoon. I'm sure that you will remember that Witness Andan testified that he had relaunched investigation in 2005, and he actively worked on that investigation about that crime. He pointed out that he had information that the crime was committed by paramilitaries, some individuals from Bijeljina, and that one such piece of information named Malovic and members of his platoon as possible perpetrators of that crime. That is on transcript pages 21825 through 21827. Based on what the Prosecutor said yesterday in the closing argument, it may be concluded that Mr. Hannis has the kind of knowledge that neither the police nor judiciary bodies have. That is why we believe that the assertion proffered by the Prosecution yesterday during their closing argument is totally arbitrary and inappropriate, as such. This claim, as the Prosecutor himself confirmed, is based on propaganda launched by a group of Chetniks in Bijeljina. According to the evidence, the MUP of Republika Srpska fought against that group, and it is more than obvious and it may be concluded that it only shows that the Chetniks sought to falsely accuse the RS MUP for a crime, and court witness Kovac also testified about that. In our final brief, in paragraphs 347 and 348, we provide the explanation for the arrival of Malovic's platoon in Bijeljina. We explained how they behaved, why they had arrived, and on whose orders. As regards the Prosecutor's position that the accused failed to undertake necessary and reasonable measures to either prevent or punish crimes committed by the police, we provide our positions in paragraphs 629 through 635 of our final brief. Yesterday, on page 76 of the transcript - and for the benefit of the interpreters, I would like to say that I'm on page 81 - the Prosecutor claimed that, based on Stanisic's actions and acts in 1994, it may be concluded that he -- that what his mens rea was in 1992, but this is obviously without any foundation. The context of 1994 was never established in these proceedings. Likewise, his mens rea in 1994 was never established because it was not relevant for the indictment period, and that's why it was never established in these proceedings. I'm sure that you will remember that the Defence asked Witness Andan to testify about the facts -- about the facts after 1992. However, the Prosecution objected to that at the time, and that is why I don't understand why the Prosecution is presenting such claims now. I suppose that according to the same principle and on the same basis following the same logic, yesterday the Prosecutor tried to draw a parallel with the laws which were passed in 1994, with regard to resubordination and the status of MUP members when they are resubordinated. The laws that were passed came into effect after the period relevant for the indictment, and that's why they cannot be of any relevance. Your Honours, I have come to the conclusion of my closing argument. I would like to conclude my closing argument - and for the benefit of the interpreters, we are on page 82 - by summarising the facts that, in our view, are relevant for your decision and put the facts within the context of the events that transpired during the time relevant for the indictment and the state of mind of the accused, Stanisic, at that time. I do not wish to deal with the matters of law because the legal practice is mostly clear when it comes to the elements of crime, as well as the necessary elements to establish the criminal responsibility of the accused. The relevant parts of our closing -- final brief which refer to those issues are paragraphs 652 through 687. As I've already stated, the context in which the processes transpired and the events in the indictment happened is very important when it comes to considering the causes of the events. The context is also very important for -- to establish the possible criminal plan and how it reflected in reality. The Prosecution -- when setting the context, the Prosecution paints a picture of normalcy in Stanisic's life. So one might be inclined to conclude that Mico Stanisic got up every morning, went to work, to the ministry, that the ministry was well organised, that the officials also came to work every day, and that they worked in their offices and their administrations or services. When the minister came, they informed him about the all the events, he briefs the heads of sectors, he issued orders, he received timely information, and he communicated constantly with the heads of the CSBs. And after the end of the working day, he went back home. However, the evidence proves beyond any doubt that just the opposite was the fact. Neither Mico Stanisic, nor a majority of the employees of the ministry had their homes, because their homes in Sarajevo, and they had fled Sarajevo. They made do as best as they can. The ministry does not operate from a single building. Actually, it operates from several building scattered all over the neighbourhood. In Pale, in the central part of the ministry, there were no offices as such. All the employees shared one or two rooms. They had one telephone which worked very erratically. They did not have means to communicate with most of the part of Republika Srpska. Of the five CSBs, three were under establishment, and the two which were in existence were completely cut off. There were, all together, 40 employees in the ministry, including drivers and administration, or administrative staff. There was no electricity. There was no paper. There were no typewriters, fuel, cars. Actually, there were no bare necessities. So this would be the true context within which the ministry headquarters operated, and this was established during the proceedings beyond in any doubt. The situation in entire Bosnia-Herzegovina is anything but normal in any sense of the word. Chaos reigned supreme and former friends and neighbours were embroiled in a civil war. There was chaos in the state and the state effectively did not exist or at least it did not function as it should have. There's no food. There's -- there are no medicines or fuel. Nothing workings as normal. Your Honour, Stanisic spent a total of 230 days in his office as minister from the 1st of April to the 24th of November when the government fell, and perhaps another month as a member of the caretaker government. When you look at the context, please bear that in mind. The Prosecutor claims that there was a criminal plan whose objective was to expel non-Serbs forcibly and permanently from the territory of the planned Serb state in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was to be done by committing crimes charged in the indictment. The Prosecutor claims that Mico Stanisic was a prominent member of this criminal association and that he considerably assisted in the implementation of the criminal plan. The Defence claims that such a criminal association never existed and if it had existed, then Mico Stanisic was not a member of such an association, nor was he aware of it, nor was he guilty of doing something or omitting to do something to -- contributed to such a plan. If such a criminal association did exist, Mico Stanisic, if he did anything, he just hindered its implementation. Your Honours, the accused and the Defence sincerely regret every innocent victim of this war; however, a possible responsibility for any crime by any individual has to be proven beyond any reasonable doubt. Your Honours, if, as the Prosecution claims, it is true that Stanisic was a member of a criminal association who significantly contributed and assisted to the commission of the criminal plan in such ways as they claim he did, then, in our view, the Prosecution had to explain to the Trial Chamber the following acts of Mico Stanisic which I will briefly list now. Firstly, the Prosecution would have to explain to the Trial Chamber why Mico Stanisic, if he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise, and if he significantly contributed to it, why, in his inauguration speech he insisted on professionalism of the police and a strict application of the law without any influence of the politics. Several days after that in Sokolac during a troop review, he repeated this again, and he emphasised the obligation to protect the public law and order and security of all people living in the territory of Republika Srpska. Further, why did Mico Stanisic in his orders, from the first to the last, which have been admitted into evidence, request conduct in accordance with the law, the regulations, and insist on criminal and disciplinary responsibility of the RS MUP employees? Further, why did Mico Stanisic send inspectors throughout Republika Srpska with the task to set up public security stations, Security Services Centres, and, in doing so, fight all sorts of crime, even at the cost of their own lives? Further, why did Mico Stanisic, if he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise to which he significantly assisted, draw up an instruction that the war crimes be documented and investigated; and why did the RS MUP issue compulsory forms in order to inform all the employees about these sort of activities that the RS MUP was engaged in at the time? Further, why did Mico Stanisic request and order that certain paramilitary formations -- or, rather, not certain, but all paramilitary formations be routed and their members arrested and prosecuted? And, to that effect, he sent the RS MUP employees to fight paramilitaries and arrest them in Brcko, Bijeljina, Zvornik, Foca, Rudo, Visegrad. Why did Mico Stanisic request the assistance of the federal SUP, and why does he request that a unit be sent to assist in that if he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise? Why did Mico Stanisic, after the arrest of the Yellow Wasps, personally go to commend the RS MUP employees for this operation, requesting that they continue to carry out tasks at the cost of their own lives? Further, when at the meeting held on the 11th of July, information was received that detention centres existed, Mico Stanisic immediately informed both the president and the prime minister about that, requesting that the situation be urgently resolved and that everything be placed within lawful framework. Two days after that, he wrote a letter to the prime minister, requesting that the government adopt a platform which would clearly express its civilised orientation and operationalise the legitimate political goals of the Serbian people, while, simultaneously, distancing itself from individuals and groups who may have different intentions, requesting at the same time that international humanitarian law and the law of war be strictly applied and war crimes be prevented. Why, in such a situation, he ordered that such detention centres, which were secured by the police, be immediately closed down and all the innocent detainees be released? Why did Mico Stanisic insist with the relevant organs that judiciary bodies be set up, both military and civilian ones, emphasising at the same time that the police could not implement laws because these bodies did not operate? Eventually, because of all this, Mico Stanisic came into conflict, as we have seen and heard from evidence, with members of the Presidency and the prime minister and was eventually relieved of his duty. So when one takes into account everything that I just listed, and I believe that the evidence proves beyond any doubt that all this was done in 1992, one may ask: How does such conduct fit with the Prosecution claim? Let me tell you: It simply does not fit. Every single of these acts is, by itself, contrary to the alleged JCE objective. If these were isolated acts and activities, one might possibly talk about an attempt to cover up the actual intentions. However, in the present instance, you can quite clearly see a pattern of behaviour which is consistent from the beginning to the end, and, clearly and directly directed against the alleged objective of the JCE and the crimes by which such an alleged objective was to be achieved. In this pattern of behaviour and the acts which he committed, there is nothing unlawful or any criminal purpose. Quite the contrary. If one compares all the minutes of collegiums held in the year 1992 and the conclusions which were adopted, it is beyond any doubt that between April and late December, he insisted on the same things, all the ones I listed. This is confirmed by the documents from the relevant period, all the witnesses we have heard, and eventually Stanisic himself in his interview. In order to illustrate this, I wanted to reading something from P190. Your Honours, this is the letter which Mico Stanisic sent on the 18th of July, one day after he sent information to the president and the prime minister with regard to the information and problems which were discussed at the first collegium of the Republika Srpska MUP. So, on the following day, he wrote a letter to Branko Djeric in which he said: "As a government member, I have repeatedly requested the drafting of a proposal of a document" -- You can see it on the screen in front of us. Can we please go on to the next slide. Further in this section he says the following: "Let me list the crimes against humanity envisaged in the international law: "War crime against civilian population. "War crime against civilian population. "War crimes against prisoners of war. "Unlawful killing and wounding of the enemy." And: "Unlawful seizure of items." So these were all the crimes that were envisaged in the rules and regulations of SFRY from the relevant field. Thirdly, he says: "In order to negate the existence of the above intent and activity, you should have proposed or initiated the establishment of a platform or another document which would present a clear and civilised implementation of what I believe are just political goals of the Serbian people. The platform ... would, at the same time, disassociate itself from all the groups and individuals with different intentions ..." Further in this section, Mr. Stanisic requests the setting up of military courts, and said: "We have many perpetrators of various crimes, a few even from the above categories, against whom measures cannot be taken as they are army members and as such fall outside the responsibility of civilians before civilian institutions." And finally, once again, here he informs the prime minister that the Ministry of the Interior is working on collecting and documenting everything relating to the crime of war crime, regardless of who the perpetrators are and what their ethnicity is. He says that he will inform about this, the Presidency, the federal SUP, and so on. Your Honours, this is a Prosecution Exhibit. I find it quite difficult to understand that, on the basis of the analysis of this document, the Prosecution failed to draw what I believe are adequate conclusions. What is the adequate and reasonable conclusion? I believe that the only reasonable conclusion is that Mico Stanisic was not a member of the JCE, if it existed at all. And not only did he not significantly assist the achievement of such an enterprise's objectives but he was evidently on the opposite side. As for the crimes of the JCE and his liability under commission through the JCE, I have discussed this in detail in our final brief and during the closing arguments when I analysed it paragraph by paragraph. And for the sake of reference, the Defence deals with this in paragraph 664 through 670 of our final brief. Also, everything that I mentioned also relates to liability for instigating or aiding and abetting. Your Honours, not only that there was no instigation in the acts of Mico Stanisic, nor was there any aiding and abetting in any of his acts, but all of them taken together, as I said, and as we have written in our final brief, are clearly directed in the opposite way. For this reason, Mico Stanisic is not criminally liable for instigating or aiding and abetting, because there is absolutely no evidence for anything like that. None of the elements necessary for the existence of those forms of liability has not been proven, including liability under commission through the JCE. As for superior responsibility, let me list, once again, the facts, some other facts, which have been established beyond any doubt during the proceedings. These are the facts that Prosecution should have explained why Mico Stanisic in a significant number of orders emphasises and insists and says, You're personally responsible. I will hold you personally responsible for the implementation of this order. This is what he says to the heads of CSBs. Why did Mico Stanisic request permanently better reporting, not just Mico Stanisic but the RS MUP as a whole? Why was an order issued to disband the so-called special units? Why were rules and instructions issued? Why did he adopt rules by which he expands disciplinary responsibility of MUP employees, at the same time imposing stricter disciplinary measures and shortening disciplinary proceedings and extending the statute of limitations. Let me dwell on this, Your Honours, because I think it is necessary that I should do so. Our final brief deals with this issue with the subtitle: Imposition of stricter disciplinary measures. Paragraphs 538 through to 563. Your Honours, during the relevant period, Mico Stanisic issued instructions that rules on disciplinary responsibility be drawn up. He added to those rules 18 new serious violations of disciplinary responsibility; 18, in total. Inter alia, omission to inform or to cover up what another employee of the MUP did. Now this is one of the serious violations. Expression of ethnic, racial, or religious intolerance. That's another one. And 16 others. In addition to this, in order to speed up disciplinary proceedings, Mico Stanisic shortened the time available for appeal from 15 days to three days, and he extends the statute of limitations from three to six months, for minor violations; and from six months to one year, for serious violations. Your Honours, in terms of standards for superior responsibility, it is our claim that the adoption of such disciplinary rules, which extend and expand disciplinary responsibility in this manner, even goes beyond the standards of what is reasonable and necessary. In addition to this, the Prosecution should have explained to us why, during the year 1992, from July onwards, Mico Stanisic relieved of their duty a significant number of employees who were members of the management staff in the RS MUP. We call -- talk about that in paragraphs 564 to 582 of our final brief. Why did he dismiss all members of the MUP who did not meet the criteria? And why did he advocate that the army should stop resubordinating MUP employees so that they could be engaged in maintaining public law and order and the security of all citizens of Republika Srpska? As with the JCE, we claim that such conduct and such behaviour, which has been established beyond any doubt during this case, shows that Mico Stanisic is not liable under superior responsibility because whatever such responsibility implies as an obligation is something that he, indeed, did do. He even did more than that. Your Honours, let's me just emphasise that, for an accused to be found culpable under superior responsibility it is necessary for him to have specific knowledge about a specific event or crime which was committed by a specific subordinate. So it has to be known directly who was the perpetrator. There are several questions which I believe we should ask at the very end. Your Honours, why does the Prosecution, in its final brief, disregard the majority of evidence presented during the trial in such a large degree? The second question: Why does the Prosecution, in its final brief, in terms of percentage, deal with the Defence case only rarely and does not suggest to you not to trust those witnesses? Then, why does the Prosecution suggest that you should not believe in Mico Stanisic's interview when it was the Prosecution evidence tendered by the Prosecution? Why does the Prosecution suggest that the evidence of all their insider witnesses should be treated in a selective manner? So why is the Prosecution trying, in essence, to minimise and limit its own case, its own evidence and its own witnesses? Well, the answer to this question, Your Honours, is because this evidence and the statements of those witnesses is the most consistent evidence in this case; because all the statements those witnesses gave primarily to the Prosecution are consistent in detail with one another. They are consistent with Mico Stanisic's interview and, what is most important, they are consistent with the written evidence from the relevant period which has been presented to you. This, Your Honours, is, in our view, the only reason. If one were to literally interpret the Prosecution claims presented during their closing arguments, they would, in fact, mean that the Prosecution suggests to the Trial Chamber not to accept the greater part of the testimony of Prosecution witnesses, and their interpretation of facts and documents relevant for this case. Instead, what is suggested to the Trial Chamber is to accept the interpretation of documents, facts, and reasons for drawing up those documents which is the result of the Prosecution reasoning and the Prosecution's understanding of their contents. On the basis of that, the Prosecution is asking you to impose a life sentence for the accused Stanisic. The Defence stands by its proposal from the final brief that Stanisic be acquitted of the charges that he committed any of the crimes under charges 1 to 10 by which he is charged in the indictment. Thank you, Your Honours. With this, I have concluded my closing arguments. I just wish to apologise once again to Ms. Korner because her intervention was justified completely, and as I am unable, at the moment to find the references that I had in mind, and as it was phrased in a different way than I intended, then I would ask you to withdraw my words from page 11 of today's transcript, line 23, to page 12, line 11. I apologise once again both to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution because of my imprecision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Let me start again. Good afternoon, Your Honours. It is a bit inconvenient to start one's closing arguments in the afternoon following my learned friends, and I hope that the closing arguments for the Defence team for Mr. Zupljanin will not make you drowsy. First of all, Your Honours, I would like to say that we are joined by other members of our team. Mr. David Martini, Lennart Poulsen, and Madam Joyce Boekestijn. Before I set out an overview of our closing arguments on behalf of our client, Stojan Zupljanin, I seize this opportunity to thank all those who assisted us in court in the course of this trial. All of us who are in this courtroom today worked well together over the course of several months. I primarily refer to interpreters, the Registry staff, security, legal officers, and other important members of the ICTY community. For this reason, my gratitude and that of the entire Defence team for Stojan Zupljanin goes to all these persons. We have also had good co-operation with the team who presented their closing arguments yesterday, as well as with other individuals who used to work with us earlier but moved to other cases subsequently. It was a honour and privilege for us to defend Stojan Zupljanin throughout this case. It is also a privilege and honour for us to be able to present our closing arguments before this Honourable Chamber. Several members of Stojan Zupljanin's Defence team will present our closing arguments. Following my introduction, Ms. Michelle Butler, our legal advisor, will first make a few preliminary remarks. She will then speak of the weight and standard of proof and address specific legal issues that we believe relevant to this case. At the very end of our closing arguments, Ms. Butler will address the issue of the sentence proposed by the Prosecution. After Ms. Butler's presentation, I will be dealing with the following topics. First, I will respond to several statements made by the Prosecution with regard to specific incidents and documents that the Prosecution placed an emphasis on in their closing arguments. I will next speak about the role of the special detachment and detention centres and about Stojan Zupljanin's alleged responsibility in connection with these centres. I will then address the take-overs in certain municipalities, and at the end of my presentation, I will speak about Stojan Zupljanin's character. My co-counsel, Aleksandar Aleksic, will be dealing with a number of different topics referred to in the Prosecution's final brief. Firstly, the credibility of specific Prosecution witnesses; then, with the alleged effective control of Mr. Zupljanin's over the perpetrators of crimes; thirdly, Zupljanin's alleged knowledge that these crimes had been committed; and, fourthly, Zupljanin's alleged failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish police crimes. I will now give the floor to Ms. Butler who will make a number of preliminary remarks relating to the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Before I begin my introductory remarks about this case, I would just like to make some brief corrections relating to the matters which Ms. Korner addressed in the beginning of her submissions on Tuesday. At transcript page 27275, my learned friend Ms. Korner mentioned that in our Defence brief there are several propositions made without any citation. She gave two examples. The first came from paragraph 1 of our brief and related to Mr. Zupljanin being an only child to a poor, rural family. The other came from paragraph 201 of our brief and related to the special police contacting Mr. Zupljanin because it was a convenient thing for them to do. Ms. Korner is right to point out these errors in our brief and we are very grateful to her for that. We would, of course, invite the Chamber to treat those as matters of submission, and, indeed, our case on Mr. Zupljanin's relationship with the special police will be developed further by my learned friend Mr. Krgovic later in these closing submissions. Ms. Korner also noted on Tuesday that there was a misleading assertion in relation to the evidence of Prosecution expert Brown. That assertion related to his views on the exceptional circumstances in which police could be resubordinated for combat activities without informing the MUP organs. The particular citation she referred to was in paragraph 235 of our final brief, and in that citation it states: "Such exceptional circumstances, i.e., war, were in fact the norm throughout the indictment period." Unfortunately, there's no reference provided for that statement in our brief. Ms. Korner -- so Ms. Korner is again quite right to pick us up on this. The fact that we don't have a reference there unfortunately implies that it was Brown who testified to that effect. We, of course, don't make that assertion. This statement was intended as a more general observation, and therefore it's right that, again, this be treated as a matter of submission, and Mr. Aleksic during the course of his submission today will be dealing more with this issue. We do, of course, sincerely apologise for these errors. It's an unfortunate fact of life that when preparing a document of this scale and nature, under very strict timelines, unfortunately, some errors of this kind inevitably creep in. For that reason, we would wholeheartedly agree with Ms. Korner's warning that the briefs invite careful reading. In fact, as Mr. Zecevic also suggested this morning, we would suggest that the Prosecution's final brief also invites very careful reading. We note, for example, that in a number of places in the Prosecution's written submissions similar errors have struck in. No doubt, entirely by accident and likely occasioned by the need to dramatically reduce word count under strict timelines. One such example of this is it in paragraph 801 of the Prosecution brief. That paragraph states in relation to crimes committed against non-Serbs at detention facilities that Mr. Zupljanin's special police followed the line of least resistance by adopting a passive stance towards crimes. For this proposition, the Prosecution cites P595 at page 4 and P624 at page 15. I won't read out the entirety of those documents due to time constraints. They're unfortunately quite long. But what I would ask is that Your Honours take a close look at them. Because on their plain meaning they show that Mr. Zupljanin was not referring to police officers taking a passive stance in relation to crimes committed at detention camps. Rather, he was referring to certain incidents at check-points, and these were check-points that paramilitaries and armed groups had been establishing and had been conducting searches of police officers. In fact, he says in those two documents that the searches -- during the searches that police officers were being mistreated. He goes on to then berate his police. He says, You're undermining their [sic] own legitimacy in the eyes of the civilian population. You are allowing yourself to be the subject of ill-treatment, and this behaviour calls into question the reputation and honour of our profession. But I won't belabour the point further before Your Honours, but the underlying message is that the Trial Chamber would benefit from a careful review of all of the transcripts and exhibits cited in the final briefs. I will now begin our closing submissions by making some introductory remarks about the context to the case and about Mr. Zupljanin in particular. Any person who has followed the more than two and a half years of this trial, no doubt, examining with great care the immense volumes of evidence from the Prosecution and the Defence that has been adduced before this Trial Chamber might expect some great rhetorical flourish or even a quotation from a famous jurist as an opening line for a closing speech. Such an approach would certainly be in keeping with many other war crimes trials in which the speeches of Robert Jackson and other great Nuremberg advocates are quoted to such an extent that they are now almost hackneyed. The Defence for Stojan Zupljanin has deliberately chosen not to take this tack. In our view, this is not a case in which a world leader used to clutching at the straws of power wishes for his lawyers to make as grand a final statement as possible in order to secure maximum coverage in the evening news. Likewise, and unlike many of the cases which Your Honours have determined in the many years of judicial experience that you have, this is not a case about a politician bent on re-writing the unfortunate events of a particular time to favour a particular ethnic bias. Rather, this case is about one man. It's about Stojan Zupljanin, a man who was a regional-level police commander in the Bosnian city of Banja Luka. This case is about the tragic events which this man who likened himself to an English Bobby was confronted in 1992. It is about the considerable efforts that he took in the face of opposition from a multitude of different entities to prevent harm to all persons in the Krajina, whether they be Serb, whether they be Muslim, whether they be Croat. In assessing this case, we say that it's critical for this Honourable Bench to take into account the catastrophe situation in which Mr. Zupljanin was forced to operate. It was a situation of war where his locality was overrun with poverty-stricken refugees. It was also overrun with criminals, criminals of all ethnicities. There was a proliferation of arms, widespread disregard for the law. There was rising banditry, rampant and escalating levels of serious crimes. In all of this, Mr. Zupljanin's subordinate officers, instead of being available to deploy at his command to prevent and punish crimes, were, for the most part, resubordinated to the army to assist in combat activities. We had said in our final brief that over 80 per cent of Mr. Zupljanin's subordinates were resubordinated during the indictment period. In fact, as we saw yesterday in -- from the extract from P2065, now that was the video in which we saw Zupljanin in 1993 giving a press conference. In actual fact, the truth figure was at least 91 per cent of his officers. Given the vastly increased crime levels and the demands of armed conflict, it's clear from this that the Banja Luka CSB was catastrophically under resourced when it was functioning with only 9 per cent of its intended capacity. The Trial Chamber has heard the considerable evidence adduced during this trial which has consistently affirmed the dire problems with communications across the RS territory. This was an unfortunate consequence brought about by the war which exasperated the considerable change already faced by Stojan Zupljanin. These challenges originated from local Crisis Staffs who took it upon themselves together with the army to usurp Mr. Zupljanin's authority and to assume control of local police to pursue their private agendas. With all the will in the world, Mr. Zupljanin was simply unable to counter their combined influence. Your Honours, the situation in which Mr. Zupljanin found himself in 1992 was ill-fated and regrettable to say the least. Despite his best intentions to protect all those around him regardless of ethnicity or religion, despite the tremendous efforts he took to try to get his subordinates to apply the law equally, some terrible crimes, crimes that scar the soul, took place on his watch. Given the array of dreadful circumstances in which Mr. Zupljanin was forced to operate, this is not surprising. We say that having an accurate understanding of this context is critical for assessing Zupljanin's alleged criminal liability. You will recall that this very point as to context was emphasised by my learned friend Mr. Krgovic during his opening statement for the Defence. At that stage, Mr. Krgovic spoke of the importance of -- that the Trial Chamber considering the wider context to the evidence presented at trial when determining the truth of this case. We maintain that, Your Honours. It's regrettable that the Prosecution apparently do not appear to consider the war time context as being of significance in their submissions. Their suggestion that Mr. Zupljanin could have stopped these dreadful crimes and could have punished the perpetrators of such acts is, with the utmost respect, naive. It is the Defence submission that they are asking of him tasks that are superhero couldn't have achieved. Given the extraordinary circumstances taking place then, no mere mortal in Mr. Zupljanin's position could have prevented and punished those crimes in the Krajina in 1992, and this is the very issue which this Trial Chamber will need to determine in its deliberations. As everyone here in this courtroom knows only too well, the mere commission of terrible crimes, and they were indeed of the most heinous kind, does not mean that everyone in the vicinity at the relevant time bears responsibility for them. In the course of this closing submission, and particularly in the submissions of my learned friends, Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Aleksic who will be dealing with the key factual allegations made by the Prosecution we will seek to illustrate that when one evaluates each transcript and each exhibit with the anxious scrutiny that it deserves, that the Prosecution have failed to discharge their heavy burden and that Stojan Zupljanin should be accordingly found not guilty on all the counts in the indictment. I will turn now, Your Honours, to the fundamental tenant of any fair system of justice: The burden and standard of proof. I make no apology for addressing this important topic despite the fact that I appear today before a Bench of professional and extremely experienced Judges. This issue, as you are no doubt well aware, should always be at the forefront of your minds. It should be there as a niggling little voice in relation to each and every element of the crimes charged. We suggest that a cursory review of the Prosecution's final brief, despite the extremely eloquent manner in which it is worded, we will deal later on with whether it's evidentially sound, we say that that brief gives one the impression that the Prosecution and the Defence are operating on some sort of evidently level playing field, that plainly is not correct. We trust that whenever Your Honours weigh two explanations of an event, applying, as it were, the scales of justice, that you place a marker on the side of the accused representing the presumption of innocence. This is because the scales of justice are not level. They are rightly tipped in favour of the accused. That is the genius of our criminal justice system in which the accused is presumed not guilty. As this Court well knows, Mr. Zupljanin does not have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt his innocence. He does not have to prove it on the balance of probabilities. In fact, Your Honours, he does not have to prove anything at all. For him to be acquitted it suffices merely that the Prosecution have not proved their case. Indeed, we say in relation to Mr. Zupljanin that the Prosecution have not proved their case in relation to any of their allegations. It is with regret that I note that on occasion our learned friends on the other side of the bar table have misapplied the burden and standard of proof. We say that such errors left unchecked by the Trial Chamber could easily result in a miscarriage of justice. One example of getting the burden ever so slightly wrong can be seen in the -- in relation to the state of communications in the Krajina in 1992. In his erudite submissions yesterday, Mr. Hannis, at T27381 said: "When the telephone didn't work, then they tried to set up a radio-relay connection. They used couriers. They delivered messages face to face. It is obvious that communications were occurring. Things weren't ideal. They never are. But we can see from the totality of the evidence that people who needed to know got the information, maybe not as quickly as they would have liked in the ideal circumstance, but it was not the situation the Defence would have you believe that some kind of prehistoric situation with no communications or a post-apocalyptic situation where everything has been destroyed and you have to resort to signal flares and smoke signs. Communications worked." Said Mr. Hannis. We suggest that stating "the Defence would have you believe" the Prosecution are applying the wrong test. The Defence are not required to have the Trial Chamber believe anything, and the Prosecution do not satisfy their heavy burden simply by asserting without any reference to particular time-periods, without reference to particular locations, that communications worked. With the greatest of respect to my learned friends, that is simply not good enough. The Prosecution must establish that the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence was that Mr. Zupljanin's ability to communicate with his subordinates and his superiors was such that at all the critical times in the indictment period, he was on notice of the crimes for which he is charged, or he could have foreseen that those crimes were likely to take place. This example demonstrates that even the most learned and even the most experienced of individuals can make errors in the application of this important concept. We seek to draw this to your attention, together with my sincere apologies to Mr. Hannis for singling him out in this way - I'm glad perhaps that he is not here at this moment - only so that such errors are not repeated by this Honourable Trial Chamber. All the Defence ask is that Your Honours judge Mr. Zupljanin solely on the facts that are proved by the Prosecution beyond a reasonable doubt because those facts argue more eloquently for his acquittal than anything that I could ever say, could do. I will turn now to my learned friend, Mr. Aleksic. No? Mr. Krgovic.
