utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] to use the time to explain to Your Honour about -- Your Honours asked about timing tomorrow. As it turns out, with the best will in the world on either side, we can't reach an exact agreement on what's to be said about the law. But, Ms. Butler, I understand, as I think Mr. Krgovic explained, is going to deal with it. Then, tomorrow, the -- the -- the two major points of this question of the interview of Stanisic. What I've already explained to Mr. Zecevic is a misunderstanding by him of what I said about it, but there's obviously what Mr. Hannis said, and, secondly this question that came up in Mr. Olmsted's review of the evidence. So I would have -- I would have thought, Your Honours, it -- it -- it probably be dealt with in about 45 minutes give or take. After the end of all the speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you indicated that, Ms. Korner, I was going to say that in terms of -- apart from any difficulty that counsel on both sides may have in terms of what you're going to do in the time, the Chamber was going to assist you by fixing a time, and I was going to say 20 minutes. But I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: At the outside, we must be completed by the time the ordinary break, so at the -- including the Judges' questions we could not exceed one session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I wasn't aware that Your Honours had any questions because do you remember I asked ages and ages ago whether that was going to happen; if so, we could have advance notice of those questions, it would assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let me rephrase what I said, including such questions as the Judges may come to appreciate tomorrow that they have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I understand that I kept Your Honours waiting. For some reason I thought you said 10 past 4.00 after all that. So I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks for the apology, Ms. Korner. But, save for your confession, we wouldn't have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Confess and avoid has disadvantages, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday the Prosecution showed in their own way and quite effectively so the crime committed at Koricanske Stijene and the supposed role and position in that of my client, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, in respect of these events. The Prosecution did so by picking out specific evidence and portions of evidence in order to place my client within the context of a joint criminal enterprise. I will now be dealing with the other part of evidence that relates to this incident but that was not shown by the Prosecution, either in their closing arguments or brief. One of the charges or accusations was that Mr. Zupljanin, in spite of the fact that there were several survivors who gave statements, could easily identify or establish the identity of perpetrators. I will now show you P1567 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rather think that might have been partly in private session, that part of the transcript. It's an exhibit but the actual part of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, but I take out all necessary --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this part of statement is without name and without any further --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner mentioned one of the survivors and the fact that he gave several statements to the judicial bodies and the police. This is a portion of the statement given by this individual referred to by Ms. Korner. Please look at what it is that the individual said when the police asked him about the identity of the perpetrators. Somebody shouted that they should come out and that an exchange was about to take place. They were lined up in two lines near a gorge, facing the gorge, and as they had to bow their heads, he saw nobody from the police, nor did he see who was lined up except for those who were closest to him. When the shooting started, he does not remember what happened afterwards. Your Honours, this was the kind of statement that all the survivors gave. In other words, none of them were able to identify the perpetrators, although they were questioned by policemen and the investigating judge. How could then Stojan Zupljanin know who the perpetrators were without resorting to some other measures? Furthermore, the Prosecution also dealt with the attitude that Mr. Zupljanin took in relation to this incident, relying on the statement of the chief of the forensic technicians team. I will present to you what it is that Mr. Zupljanin said. You had occasion to see this, not in the statement that was modified and prepared by the Prosecution, but live. Witness Pejic at transcript page 1448 said the following: [In English] "Q. What was Mr. Zupljanin's response to this? "A. When I met with chief Zupljanin in private at -- in the morning before the meeting, I noticed that he appeared to be shaken. He was visibly shaken. He condemned the incident strenuously. He called a spade a spade. He said it was a crime." [Interpretation] this is what Stojan Zupljanin said. This is the gist of his attitude towards this event -- this incident. At transcript page 1451, Witness Pejic goes on to say on the issue of how Mr. Zupljanin treated the survivors, and I quote: [In English] "A. She [sic] ordered me very strictly that I'm personally responsible for the security and safety of that person and that I should bring him as soon as is possible to the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka ... "Q. Did you discuss -- once you arrived Banja Luka did you discuss with Mr. Zupljanin what would be done with this man? "A. Yes, and he told me that he would be turned over to the Swiss Red Cross." [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are other testimonies in this case, but Zupljanin told the witness here that he did everything in his power and he would do everything in his power to make sure that all the six survivors had their wounds treated, would recover, and be handed over to the Red Cross. Had Stojan Zupljanin wanted, as the Prosecution alleged yesterday, to cover up this crime, why would he then do as he did? Why would he protect the survivors? Why would he hand them over to the Swiss Red Cross, if his intention was to cover up the crime and make sure that nobody came to know of it? Yesterday the Prosecution played a video-clip that was filmed shortly after the crime where Zupljanin spoke in public about the investigation in a way to make sure that he would not divulge any details. He did not -- not want to speak of any possible eye-witnesses, and that was only natural that a policeman would speak in such subdued terms when the investigation was still going on, and I want to recall the testimony of Mr. Krejic again in this respect because he was shown the video. At transcript page 1496 to 97, he answered to a question that was put to him: [In English] "Q. And disclosing the identity and the number of survivors of the massacre to the public would put them at risk and would jeopardy size the investigation, isn't that so? "A. Yes, well, I suppose that would be the case." [Interpretation] Your Honours, no police force in the world would, if there are survivors around who are at risk, divulge any details of the incident, and this is what Zupljanin himself made sure he did. Your Honour, the Prosecution also tried in their closing arguments yesterday to present the police force as not having done their job properly. Neither in this case, nor in the case of killings or murders in Vrbas does that apply. Perhaps this would be the case in an ideal world, but not in Banja Luka, in the area of Krajina in the course of 1992. A Prosecutor who was seized of both these cases testified before this Tribunal. I will present to you what it is that he said about the work of the Banja Luka services centre and, in my view, he is much better placed to speak -- than the Prosecution to speak of the abilities of the CSB Banja Luka in this criminal period, and he said, I will quote: [In English] "Q. But we would agree that the operative officer in CSB Banja Luka, under the circumstances, did everything to document the crime and created a basis for eventual closure of the case 18 years later." Said: "A. Yes." And furthermore, Your Honour, [Interpretation] When our learned friend Mr. Pantelic, whom we all miss, as Ms. Korner said herself, when he asked the witness whether the Prosecution did everything in their power to investigate and adequately process those crimes, let me remind to look at transcript page 14292 and 293. You will see what he answered. He said clearly that he as a prosecutor personally considers that he could have done more. Your Honours, the Prosecution, when saying that nothing was done after October 1992 also stated that it was, indeed, possible and I would like to remind you of a testimony we heard in this case where members of the unit who were involved in the crime were deployed and assigned to a -- military units at least until the end of 1992, and they were not available to the police bodies, despite all the efforts made by Stojan Zupljanin in order to learn their identity and in order to bring them in. And let me just remind this Trial Chamber, today, 20 years after the crime, the proceedings are still under way based the evidence that was collected by the CSB at the time and based on the criminal report that was filed by nobody else but Stojan Zupljanin himself. And then when it reached the hands of a more capable prosecutor, has this criminal report been processed in a more appropriate way? Moreover, the Prosecutor showed you a document yesterday. According to the Prosecutor, that document reveals some of the positions of Stojan Zupljanin. The number of that document is P583. I would like to call up the document. We were not able to present it as a PowerPoint document, so I would like to call it up in e-court. I would like to display page 2 in this document and the same page in the English version as well. Your Honour, here the Prosecutor claims that Stojan Zupljanin resisted -- or, rather, he demonstrated his discriminatory intent. The gist of the document is this: Mr. Zupljanin expressed his dissatisfaction with several things. Under 1, the police being used to secure and guard people who were detained in this manner, and he believes, and there's a word here in which -- which in our language has a totally different meaning. And it was translated as hostages, "totci" [phoen] in Serbian, "hostages" in English. Hostages sounds horrible in English. However, I'm going to show you another document. This applies to people who were unlawfully detained without any foundation or grounds for their detention. And it is used --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, this is obviously an important document, that's why I raised it. It is not for Mr. Krgovic to give evidence as to meaning. If he says that is the wrong translation, the word is not hostages, it should have been raised some time ago and it should be raised now. It is not for Mr. Krgovic to say this is the wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe Ms. Korner was not listening carefully. I'm not talking about mistranslation or misinterpretation. I was talking about the way, this expression, or term, or word may be interpreted, may be explained. You will see later on, you will see there is another term used for this category of people and the term is "isolated." They were isolated. What I'm trying to say with this is that this document should be interpreted in its entirety and in relation to other documents, and when the Prosecutor showed his PowerPoint, and I don't know whether there was a mistake in interpretation, and when Mr. Zupljanin asked for something that can be seen on the following page of the document that we have on the screen now - can we go to the following page, please - when he requested something and the prosecutor said that Zupljanin requested an action to be taken, whereas, in this document, it says a clear position. Be it as it may, I'm going to show you what the position of Stojan Zupljanin was with regard to this category of people and what actions he called for in relation to these people. Your Honour, yesterday the Prosecutor addressed you and showed you a document that I would like to call up now. This is P750. You see, Your Honours, this is a document issued by the War Presidency of Kljuc municipality. In this document, the Presidency informed the CSB about people who were released from Manjaca and who belonged to the category referred to by Mr. Zupljanin. The Prosecutor used this document to show that the War Presidency did not have control over public security stations but that it was the other way around; that War Presidencies actually implemented Zupljanin's order. This is what the Prosecution tried to demonstrate using this document. And this is a trick. Because if you look at this document in isolation, on its own, you might arrive at that conclusion. However, look at the document that precedes this document, which is P607. This is the initial document that's -- that Stojan Zupljanin dispatched. Look at the heading. It says, "To the chief of the public security station." And then the chief of the public security station, instead of replying to Stojan Zupljanin or taking any kind of measures, actually went to his own War Presidency, and the War Presidency then answered Stojan Zupljanin by saying the public security station is not capable of taking the necessary measures. And, here, Your Honours, from this letter, you will see what the position of Stojan Zupljanin was with regard to these categories of individuals. In the third paragraph from the top where it says: "However, there is some information that indicates that [word illegible]." It should be isolated individuals this is a bad translation, and this is the category that existed in our system. And as Mr. Zecevic said, the Prosecutor did not interpret the legal terms and the legal system in the way it existed in the former Yugoslavia because in the former Yugoslavia, in the Yugoslav legal practice, the term "isolated persons" or "hostages," we all know that it was illegal to keep hostages but this refers to people who were detained or kept without any grounds for that. And what is the position of Stojan Zupljanin with this regard? Let me remind you. It says: "To their obligation to take proportionality measures to protect these individuals, guard their houses and property, and prevent any attempt at threatening or in any other way intimidating these people." Or applying force against them. Moreover it says: "Any possible incident, event, attack, or any other form of threat against these people should be thoroughly analysed by operational, tactical, and criminal experts. Everything should be recorded and the necessary measures taken to identify and arrest the perpetrators of these crimes." And then Mr. Zupljanin went on to present his categorical position vis-a-vis these people: "In co-operation with municipal bodies, the Red Cross organisation, humanitarian organisations, and other bodies, if necessary, these people should be provided with food, accommodation, medical and other forms of help" when they returned to their former places of residence. What I'm saying with this, Your Honours, may be taking it much further than Ms. Butler said. When you judge Stojan Zupljanin, when you make a decision on his responsibility, and I am taking this further, you should not be reading the Prosecutor's final brief carefully. What I am saying is that you should not even attempt to read that part that speaks about the responsibility of Stojan Zupljanin. Instead you should be reading the evidence. Because the technique of taking things out of the context, taking documents out of the context and linking them up in the way it was done in the Prosecutor's final brief is not going to amount to much, and it's not going to take you anywhere. Moreover, Your Honours, the Prosecution, in their final brief, and yesterday in their closing argument dealt with what happened in Prijedor during the take-over. And yesterday the Prosecutor showed you an excerpt from Simo Drljaca's document about the number of policemen and the way the power was taken over. I invite you to read this document, and when you do this, could you please also refer to the testimony of Witness Jankovic who commented upon this document when asked about the number of police officers. He says, when it comes to the number of police officers: [In English] "as a [indiscernible] dispatches, I think it tallies with my figures, more or less, according to the books, but as of for his numbers of policemen, et cetera, no way. 1300 policemen? Where did you come up with that? No way. It's an exaggeration. Before the war, entire station had 230 employees ..." [Interpretation] And when you judge the possible role that the police played in the take-over of power in Prijedor, please bear this testimony in mind. Your Honours, and now I'm going to address another topic, and that's the special unit of the police, and since both the Defence and the Prosecution in their brief -- final briefs and the Prosecution in their final -- closing argument dealt with that unit, if you looked at the documents that were presented and that were highlighted by the Prosecutor, you will see that the two documents that were presented were issued at the beginning of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you will see when that unit was actually established. That unit was established at the moment when nobody actually knew what the role of the JNA would be in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina because the JNA was in the processes of withdrawing and the Army of Republika Srpska had not been established yet. That is why the Assembly of the ARK and not the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska issued a decision in order to establish that unit because only the MUP of Republika Srpska had the authority to establish such a unit, but he failed to do that. From the evidence presented by the Prosecutor, you saw that the CSB played a certain role in the setting up of that unit. However, when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, it is our position that both the structure and the goals, as well as the composition of that unit were changed, and that is why the unit became predominantly a military unit. This shows that that unit was composed mostly of the troops and a minority of the police officers who had the necessary experience. The formal or the official commander of that unit was Captain Lukic. He was appointed by Colonel Stevilovic. The organisation of the unit as described by several witnesses in this case and I would like to highlight Witness SZ-02 [as interpreted] on transcript pages 25419, 25418 and 25655. Moreover, the Prosecution say in their final brief that Ecim and Samardzija were members of the SDB and that they were factually the detachment commanders after Captain Lukic was injured in a traffic accident in late May. This claim, Your Honours, is a far cry from the truth. When you listen to the testimony of Witness Gajic who spoke about the disbanding of the unit and when you saw who were the people who were present there at the time and let me remind you who were. You will find that on transcript page T10760 and 10796. The commander of the unit at that meeting was there, and he objected to the disbanding of the unit. If you pay attention to the testimony of Witness Tutus, transcript page 968, you will see that in July 1992, the commander of the unit, Captain Lukic, together with Captain Dubocanin exerted pressure on Tutus to release the arrested unit members. So the unit had its commander all the time. Perhaps he was absent for a while, but you can see him throughout the period in which

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 721 and 833 of the Prosecution final brief, it is claimed that Zupljanin was authorised by the minister to set up, equip, finance and maintain special units of the CSB. Of course, this is not contained in any document. A document which has to do with the reorganisation of the MUP because of the war conditions is the one that is quoted by the Prosecution. Further, in paragraph 748, the Prosecution claims that, I quote: "Zupljanin must have been aware of the activities of these police units on the basis of regular reports and meetings with SJB chiefs." Once again, a term that my learned friend, Ms. Butler, dealt with, that he must have -- he must have been aware. In this trial, Your Honour, after the outbreak of conflict in May 1992, there was just one collegium held on the 30th of July, 1992, which was held -- and Zupljanin's urgent reaction on the basis of what he learned at the meeting is contained in Exhibit 2D25. It is a document that was drawn up on the very same day. In paragraph 974 of the Prosecution final brief, the Prosecution claims that Zupljanin ordered the release of two members of the special police from the Banja Luka prison. If you have look at what witnesses ST-123 said on transcript page 7968 and Witness SZ-002 on transcript page 25713 and 25714, who requested that these men be released and what Zupljanin essentially wanted, and it was not that the men be released but that they be handed over to the judiciary organs in order to avoid a conflict between the army and the police. Your Honours, let me not deal any further with the claims in which the Prosecutor talked about the links between the CSB and this unit because I think we have already said quite a lot about that in our own final brief. Only when it comes to the link this is the paragraph 723 of the final brief about the SOS and Zupljanin's relation to them. Let me quote Witness ST-123 on transcript page 7780 and 7652 when he talked about engaging SOS with the police and when he said that Zupljanin was against members of the SOS joining the police but that he was unable to prevent this. Further, in paragraph 738 of the Prosecution final brief, Witness ST-197 is quoted. The Prosecution uses his words to illustrate that Slobodan Dubocanin was never placed under the command of the 22nd Light Brigade. The Defence claims that Slobodan Dubocanin, firstly, never was a member of the special unit, that he was a member of the army, holding the rank of captain, who spent late summer and early fall of 1993 under the direct command of the commander of the 22nd Light Brigade; exhibit which I refer you to is 2D63. Please have a look at this, Your Honours. This is Slobodan Dubocanin file card. You have had the occasion to see it. From the 12th of September, 1992, up until the 20th of October, 1992, he is in the military post 7404, Knezevo. The claims of Witness ST-197 were directed at evading his known responsibility for the actions of units which were subordinated to him. My learned friend, Mr. Aleksic, will talk more about this. You have heard that most of the criminal activities committed in Kotor Varos could be traced back precisely to Slobodan Dubocanin and his unit. Further, Your Honours, the Defence also wants to clarify a dilemma which the Prosecution may have about our position with regard to the alleged murders in front of the health centre in Kotor Varos. Firstly, in order to make myself entirely clear, the Defence claims that the special unit did not have anything to do with the murder committed in front of the health centre and that during its cross-examination of eye-witnesses, it opposed the claims that the special unit was involved in this crime. Your Honours, the Prosecution founded the count of the indictment relating to this event on three documents. The first of these are the minutes from the Crisis Staff meeting in Kotor Varos, P46. The second is P1790 which is a report of the 2nd Krajina Corps. And, finally, a report of the so-called expert Brown who erroneously linked these two documents in the Talic case and whose work from the Talic case was admitted into evidence in this case. So, to make myself clear, the incident about which the first document talks, the one from the Crisis Staff, was the most difficult day in Kotor Varos when there were six dead Serbs and some wounded who were brought to the health centre. That was one incident. Another incident was the massacre against special police members which happened on the following day and about which the 1st Krajina Corps reports. And the third incident is the murder in front of the health centre which occurred between these two dates. And this is what Brown accepted as his wrong conclusion; namely that these were three separate incidents. The Defence only tried to prove during the cross-examination of the survivor that the special unit was not involved in the incident but that the incident was committed by the locals, and we deal with this in our final brief. Further, Your Honours, yesterday the Prosecution, and the day before yesterday as well, the Prosecution showed you some photos from Kotor Varos - actually, one photo - on which one can see men with red berets walking down a street as if they were models. No shooting is going on. There are no signs of combat, and I recall that when this exhibit was shown to SZ-02, this is what he said on transcript page 25818. This man, whom the Prosecution showed to you yesterday walking around and these other men were not members of the unit because the Prosecution also showed you the film of the parade with the unit members. Did you see any red berets among the members of the special unit from the month of May? Did you see any green uniforms in this video-clip? Your Honour, I will now be dealing with the Defence position in respect of detention centres. It relates to paragraph 761 of the Prosecution final brief, where it is asserted that the Manjaca camp was, in fact, a police facility, although it was primarily secured by the army. The Prosecution -- the Defence want to recall the Prosecution witness, ST-172, transcript page T5266 and page T5267. This testimony will clearly indicate who had the authority over Manjaca. The witness confirmed that at no point did a single civilian policemen enter the camp because all the policemen who were ever there to secure the camp had been resubordinated. It is the position of the Defence, which is firmly supported by evidence, that the civilian police, who accompanied -- or were the escort of the prisoners -- they were guarding the prisoners were resubordinated and were given an assignment that fell outside the scope of activity of the Ministry of the Interior. The relevant reference is Witness ST-139, transcript 8691; ST-172, transcript 5281; P1284.55; and 1D43. On the issue of Prijedor, which we addressed extensively in our final brief, I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of the Prosecution's position that Stojan Zupljanin was informed of the situation in the camps in Prijedor. Let me say what Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the code-name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- said at transcript T2116, where he clearly said that Drljaca and Bera misled Zupljanin deliberately by feeding him misinformation. Let me tell you precisely what the witness said: [In English] "... that Simo Drljaca, Vojin Bera and others painted an untruthful picture of the events that were taking place in the area. They painted a picture that was much softer in terms of consequences. They were doctoring information, and they could have prevent the crimes which have been established in their number and nature in both Omarska and in Keraterm and in the general area of Prijedor municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the pseudonym of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was Witness Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I disclosed a couple of names a moment ago, I am now using their pseudonyms in order to avoid any inadvertent mistakes. At paragraph 763 of the Prosecution final brief where the mistreatment of prisoners at Teslic is discussed, the Prosecutor maintains that Zupljanin did nothing upon learning of the mistreatment of prisoners in the SJB building in Teslic. Your Honours, can anything be further from the truth than this statement by the Prosecution? We have heard here countless testimonies about how Zupljanin organised the Mice Group's arrest in Teslic, how he removed the chief of the public security and the commander of the station, Markovic, for their failure to protect the non-Serbs, and he appointed Radulovic as acting chief of public security station. He undertook a criminal procedure against them and secured the release of the Croats and Muslims from detention. Perhaps we found ourselves in different places, we and the Prosecution, since the Prosecution dare to come up with a statement such as this one. Your Honours, as for Sanski Most, I will not be dealing with this in detail as it has been addressed in our final brief, but it is obvious that all the evidence related to this territory demonstrates that Zupljanin had no authority over detention centres in Sanski Most or any other detention locations in that town. This applies to Kljuc as well, where there is only one post festum report, which is P96024, where Chief Kondic says that there are reasons to undertake criminal proceedings against all these men and they should be prosecuted for the crimes they committed and they should be prosecuted before a military court as soon as may be. Donji Vakuf we addressed it in our final brief was under military administration and document 19 -- or, rather, P1927 clearly indicates that the detention or the collection centre in Vakuf was set up in the month of May by the command of the 19th Partisan Brigade. And this claim that all the detention centre in Republika Srpska were under police authority is absurd. In paragraph 367, the Prosecutor says that Zupljanin allowed the mistreatment of prisoners in CSB and they quote ST-27 as their reference. I appeal to Trial Chamber to look carefully at what this witness said at T747, 748, and onwards. In paragraph 795 of the Prosecution final brief, the Prosecution claim that Zupljanin conveyed the 10 August order to Stanisic with a delay to carry out the transfer of the camp to the army and that he delayed it until the end of August. The Defence is of the position that there was no delay. The order was conveyed on the 19th of August. Only nine days later, upon receipt of that order, in view of the state of war and the fact that the communications system was not operational, the time-period was reasonable. I will give you an illustration, just as my learned friend Mr. Zecevic showed you an example at the level of Republika Srpska, at the Banja Luka CSB, based on exhibits and evidence, what the scope of communications was in 1992 compared to 1991. Here you have the relevant figures. Your Honours, I will now move to a different topic, namely the takeover of municipalities and the division of public security stations. The Defence is of the view that the division of SJBs and takeovers of municipalities were two completely separate processes. We want to highlight this. Zupljanin's participation in peace negotiations was in contradiction from the very start to the actions taken by the Crisis Staff and the army. Zupljanin met regularly with municipal leaders of different ethnicities long before the start of the armed conflict and encouraged co-operation between different ethnic groups in order to reduce tensions. At paragraph 129, the Prosecution, yet again, misquote -- misquote evidence when referring to Zupljanin's contact with SOS and quote Witness Radulovic, they take his sentence out of context. Radulovic clearly said who it was he considered was close to SOS. He said, Kesic, my head of the security service. And where is Zupljanin in this? And Zupljanin is being mentioned in that context by the Prosecution. Your Honour, I will not dwell on Sanski Most or the takeover of municipalities because I am pressed for time. We dealt with these matters in detail in our brief. I would like to show up -- or, actually to refer you to P390. This is the chief of the public security station Sanski Most sending a letter to Zupljanin, wherein it is said the Sanski Most police was not deployed nor did it take part in the combat activities that were carried out by the armed force -- by the parties to the conflict because they did not have the necessary training, nor was that the purpose that they served. Let me go back to Kljuc and give you another example, Your Honours, of this cherry picking of specific portions of testimony that are then taken out of context. In paragraph 378, the Prosecution quote what -- what a witness said, and it was said that Zupljanin said that by the 2nd of May, the change of uniforms was already a done deal and nothing could be done about it. But, in fact, if you look at the following response, at page 4745 to 9, you will see what it was that the witness said when he spoke about Zupljanin. It was our understanding that he wanted to say that he was unable to take a decision, one way or the other, because some other persons or other organs were the ones who had already made a decision on this issue. We spoke to a person who was in no way able to assist us in that matter. Your Honours, at paragraph 392 of the Prosecution final brief, it is stated in reference to Zupljanin that both he and Kondic knew that the police helped the army to arrest people. There is evidence that indicates that Kondic informed the chief, Zupljanin. Let's see where do we find this evidence. Transcript page 15980, Witness ST-218. His Honour Delvoie asked him the following. And it's about Biljane. The witness said: "We did not investigate into this further because it was committed by the army, and criminal reports were already filed. It was a -- well-known who it was who perpetrated these crimes and we did not investigate them. Chief Kondic was aware of it and probably through a regular report he informed the chief of the centre, but this is only a conclusion on my part." His Honour Judge Delvoie said: "You said probably so you're not quite sure. "A. I am not sure because we never mentioned that topic." Furthermore, another example of how the Prosecution created their final brief and how they interpreted evidence. That's paragraph 456, where they claim and they say: "In early April a meeting was held at the CSB Banja Luka where Zupljanin explained to the leadership of Kotor Varos that all policemen had to sign a pledge of loyalty to the RS. Although the meeting was supposed to resolve any conflicts that may arise due to request, Zupljanin did not offer any comprise and addressed Djukanovic. "President, bang your fist and resolve this situation. Zupljanin then said: "Allow Nedeljko Maric to be the chief of the Croats, Muhamed Sadikovic to lead the Muslims and Savo Tepic to lead the Serbs." All in all, those present, the context and the meaning that the Prosecution reads into this meeting are completely erroneous. Djekanovic was not at this meeting. He is not there. Look at what witness 258 said about who met with Zupljanin on that day. Transcript page 17542 to 17544. There, you will kind, and I quote:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really sorry but private session testimony is not testimony that is open to the public. Parts are quoted in final brief because it's -- they are all confidential final briefs. This is a public session. The reason that private session testimony is in private session is -- is so that it's not going out to the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Krgovic, perhaps the course that you should take is -- I assume that this is incorporated into your own brief and you need merely in these public sessions draw the Chamber's attention to the particular parts of your brief, but out of an abundance of caution, I think we will redact that -- that portion of what you have just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I follow your suggestion. This part, particularly, wasn't incorporated in our final brief because that was first time we were aware when Prosecution quoted this particular piece of evidence in his own final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you assist me and the Court Officer with the lines, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ... it's line -- sorry, it's page 112 from effectively line 4 through to the end of whatever Mr. Krgovic quoted. Line 11, we think. No, it's goes on further. All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, so that will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are many such examples of misinterpreting evidence and taking things out of the context. My colleague Mr. Aleksic will go on and deal with some other matters but let me repeat what I already stated at the beginning of my presentation. Look at the evidence when it comes to the responsibility of Stojan Zupljanin. Do not read the Prosecutor's final brief. Look at the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour there are two matters that I really need to deal with. I don't know whether it would be appropriate to deal with them now or whether at the end of the day or tomorrow. I would submit that it is probably better to deal with then now. One of them goes back to Mr. Krgovic who is giving evidence about translations. The is in relation to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we confirm from Mr. Krgovic that we are effectively at the end of the day. I thought he was about to hand over to Mr. Aleksic. In which case the few remaining minutes we can deal with -- with these matters if you wish to raise. Is that where we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have finished my part of the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so Mr. Krgovic will take the baton -- Mr. Aleksic will take the baton tomorrow morning. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- if we go back, please, to what Mr. Krgovic was saying at page 96 of today's transcript -- sorry. It's maybe ... Actually, it's before 96 where he is dealing with the document I raised yesterday, P583. It's the next document there I've marked up ... Page -- I'm sorry. Thank you very much. It's page 93, Your Honours. I'm sorry, I failed to mark it. Yes. P53. And this is, Your Honours, where I objected. He says that he is going to show you another document that applies to people who are unlawfully detained without any foundational grounds for their detention. It is not much better but it's not what hostage means, as Your Honours know. Your Honours, before we dealt with that document because it was such an important document we had double-checked, as far as we're concerned, that that was the correct translation. No one has, throughout this trial, and this document is a reasonably early document, I think it may have come in through Mr. Nielsen, suggested that that was a wrong translation. It is therefore not for Mr. Krgovic to give evidence that it has a completely separate meaning and to go on to compound the offence of giving evidence by purporting to read what has been said in the B/C/S to be -- and English an illegible part of a document which is P601. That's what he mentioned at page 96, where he purports to give a translation going along this theme of what this particular word is, or a different word, but that translation does not appear. We have the hard copy of it. It's illegible. So we say Your Honours cannot take that into account. The evidence is closed. If the Defence want to file an application to re-open the case to deal with that, they can do so. But we invite Your Honours to totally disregard what Mr. Krgovic has said about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- the short response, I suppose, Ms. Korner, is that that would be the course that the Chamber would take. But unless I misunderstood Mr. Krgovic, he seemed to have - and you would both correct me if I'm wrong -- he seemed to have -- resiled would be the wrong word, but modified, as it were, his challenge to the mistranslation because as you have indicated, the proper course would be to make the appropriate application and where I understood him to -- to place himself was that the inference -- the understanding -- I don't want to use the word "interpretation," I don't want to use the word "inference" because it is neither of those, but the understanding taken as a whole, and I'm putting aside wholly what you have just indicated would have been his interpelations of illegible parts in the B/C/S that he read in the record, let's ignore that. But what I understood his position to become was that we read the document and this is, in fact, the effect. So in other words it's a type of argument which could be properly advanced even if translation wasn't involved at all. We have a document in -- in say, English and everybody is an English speakers and counsel A says, This is the interpretation that you, the Trial Court, should find. The other side says the opposite. That's what I understood him to be at the end of the day. But if I got to wrong then, of course, the Chamber need simply ignore the -- his -- his effective supplementing of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I would admit that when I got up to object to this but except that he went on this, and this was the part at page 96, to draw the analogy from document P601 where he says it should -- it says, "word illegible" should be "isolated individuals." This is a bad translation. This is the -- I may say it's not the clearest what he is saying. This is the category that existed in our system, and as Mr. Zecevic said, the prosecutor did not interpret the legal terms and the legal system in the way it existed in the Yugoslav legal practice. The term "isolated persons" or "hostages," we all know that it was illegal to keep hostages, but this refers to people who were detained or kept without any grounds for that. Your Honour, it's of course for Your Honours to read the context of the term "hostages" but what now seems to be suggested is that Your Honours should take into account, about which again you've heard no evidence, something about the Yugoslav legal practice. We say the word is "hostages." It is it properly interpreted and the context makes it clear and Mr. Krgovic cannot seek to go behind that by giving evidence. And that's the first thing. Did Your Honours want to hear from Mr. Zecevic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Krgovic on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you understood me well when it comes to the first objection by Ms. Korner. I didn't say that was it a wrong translation but it was the literal translation and that the meaning of that term had to be put in the context of our formal legal systems. What it meant and how we used it, that was the meaning of my interjection. Because the term was not mistranslated. It was literally translated. I did not object, I did not claim that the translation was wrong. Not for a moment that was my position or intention. And when it comes to the second document that I read from the screen, in the Serbian when I read, the document reads "isolation," and that is why it should be re-sent for translation because it is very important that this document be put in the context of my whole presentation. I presented my position with regard to this document and how it should be (a) translated; (b) interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours -- Your Honours, that's the problem. We have had no evidence at all about how that term should be applied in the previous -- or was applied in the previous Yugoslav system. So, therefore, we submit that Your Honours should ignore Mr. Krgovic's submissions on this point because that is giving evidence. And, literally, the word is "hostages." Your Honours can see the context, and it's a matter for Your Honours to decide what's meant by that. I think that's as far as I can take that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your second point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second point relates to Kotor Varos and Mr. Brown. Mr. -- and they did the same in their brief. Mr. Krgovic said -- and this is at page 104, I think. Takes it -- found a mistake. Yes, page 104, line 10. Where Mr. Krgovic says he is going to clarify the dilemma which the Prosecution may have about the -- the Defence, Prosecution, in regard to the health centre killings. And he says that we founded the count of the indictment on the killings outside the health centre and assert that it was committed by the special police on the Kotor Varos minutes of meetings; P46. We do not, Your Honour, we never have, and in the final brief, it is P81 -- can we -- can I ask for it to be put up. P46 is a totally different thing. Your Honours, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this. This is rebuttal. Ms. Korner should not be allowed to present her position on this occasion. She shouldn't be allowed to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to correct a total misrepresentation of the evidence. It has nothing do with rebuttal. I am saying that Mr. Krgovic, by saying that we found this on P46, is deliberately, as they did in their final brief, misrepresenting the evidence, first of all, of Mr. Brown, and secondly, of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, you don't have the procedural right to respond to that. You could do that in your final brief, in your closing argument, because we represented my position in our final brief and during our case and the presentation of evidence in our case, and we only repeated it during our closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krgovic, if Ms. Korner claims that the correct reference should have been Exhibit P81 and not P46, would you agree to that? Then we can settle the issue here and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. My reference was to P46. I did not mention P81.

utterances.text: I know you did not mention P81. But I think the issue is here that a possible mistake may have been made by you by quoting 46 rather than 81. So if that was a mistake, then we can settle it. If not, then it is subject to --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will check whether that is the case. I will respond tomorrow. I'm not sure. The case is that Mr. Brown associated them erroneously with that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- I'm perfectly happy -- we've dealt with -- with -- or I dealt with that in my final address on this. That's all -- the rest, leaving -- is for Your Honours to decide, having read that. But it is totally erroneous to say that we base our allegation of the crime committed by the special police on P46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And to that extent, it should be patent from your final briefs. So there's -- there's nothing for us to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krgovic. It is not right that in a public speech Mr. Krgovic should make a total misrepresentation of what our case is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I must say, I must remind Ms. Korner of her claim. I'm listening to the way the evidence was presented by the Prosecution. I'm qualified to assess what the Prosecutor's case against my client is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we can't take this matter any further [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No -- but, Your Honour, no, I -- I -- very well. But I want it just very clear. As I say, this is in public, and I think it's right, at no stage have we ever said that anything other than P81 was the basis for the allegation -- the later, accepted misunderstanding by Mr. Brown of the later document, which Mr. Krgovic showed Mr. Brown, is right.
